parts.problemMd:
Given that $\left(8 - \sqrt{x}\right) \left(5 + \sqrt{x}\right) = y \sqrt{x} + 21$  where $x$ is a prime number and $y$ is an integer,

find the value of $x$ and the value of $y$.

Show each stage of your working clearly.

x = .............................................................

y = ............................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> *Expand the two brackets/factors on the left hand side.*

$\left(8 - \sqrt{x}\right) \left(5 + \sqrt{x}\right) = 40 + 8 \sqrt{x} - 5 \sqrt{x} - \left(\sqrt{x}\right)^{2}$

> *Simplify as far as possible.*

$40 + 8 \sqrt{x} - 5 \sqrt{x} - \left(\sqrt{x}\right)^{2} = 40 + 3 \sqrt{x} - x$

**[1]**

> *Now compare the left hand side and right hand side of the equation.*

$40+3\sqrt{x}-x=y\sqrt{x}+21$

> *The constant parts should be equal.*

$\begin{aligned}40 - x & = & 21 \\ x & = & 19\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*(This meets the requirement that **x** is a prime number.)* *The "*$\sqrt{x}$*" terms should also be equal.*

$\begin{aligned}3 \sqrt{x} & = & y \sqrt{x} \\ y & = & 3\end{aligned}$

$x=19,y=3$** [1]**

> *Although this may at first appear to be a quadratic equations question, it's actually a linear equations question "in disguise"!*

> *Expand the brackets, noting that *$\left(2 x + 5\right)^{2} = \left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x + 5\right)$*.*

$4x^{2}+10x+10x+25=4x^{2}-2x+6x-3$

**[1]**

> *Collect like terms on both sides.*

$4x^{2}+20x+25=4x^{2}+4x-3$

> *Now subtract *$4x^{2}$* from both sides, to reveal the linear equation!*

$\begin{aligned}4 x^{2} + 20 x + 25 & = & 4 x^{2} + 4 x - 3 \\ - 4 x^{2 } & = & - 4 x^{2} \\ 20 x + 25 & = & 4 x - 3\end{aligned}$

> *Solve the linear equation. Subtract *$4x$* from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}16 x + 25 & = & - 3\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract 25 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}16 x & = & - 28\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 16.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{- 28}{16} = - \frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}$

$x=-\frac{7}{4}$ ** [1]**

**−1.75 is accepted**

$12x^{2}+12$* ***[1]**

*Following the "or otherwise", write out the squared brackets as the product of two brackets* * *

$\left(x^{2} + 4\right) \left(x^{2} + 4\right) - \left(x^{2} - 2\right) \left(x^{2} - 2\right)$ * *

$( x^{4} + 4 x ^{2} + 4 x ^{2} + 16 ) - ( x^{4} - 2 x ^{2} - 2 x ^{2} + 4 )$
$= ( x^{4} + 8 x ^{2} + 16 ) - ( x^{4} - 4 x ^{2} + 4 )$

**[1]**

*Remove the brackets (by multiplying all terms by -1 in the second bracket)* * *

**[1]**

> *Collect like terms*

parts.problemMd: Factorise   $3x^{2}+14x+8$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The coefficient of the *$x^{2}$* term is not 1 so you can factorise the expression by grouping and factorising.*

> *Find the product of the coefficient of the *$x^{2}$* term and the constant term.*

$3\times8=24$

> *Find the factor pairs of this product.*

$1,24\mathrm{or}-1,-24\,2,12\mathrm{or}-2,-12\,3,8\mathrm{or}-3,-8\,4,6\mathrm{or}-4,-6$

> *Find the factor pair that adds together to give you the same value as the coefficient of the *$x$* term.*

$2,12:2+12=14$

> *Rewrite the original expression splitting up the *$x$* term using the values determined above.*

$3x^{2}+2x+12x+8$

> *Group the terms into two pairs, the first two terms as one pair and the last two terms as the second pair. *

> *Factorise both pairs of terms.*

$x \left(3 x + 2\right) + 4 \left(3 x + 2\right)$

> *Both terms in the expression have a factor of *$\left(3 x + 2\right)$*, so can now be factorised with this as the common factor.*

$(3x+2)(x+4)$

**Factorisation to **$\left(3 x + a\right) \left(x + b\right)$** where **$ab=8$** or  **$a+3b=14$** ****[1] ****Fully correct factorisation**** [1]**

parts.problemMd: Factorise  $x^{2}--11x+24$
parts.solutionMd:
*Find two numbers that multiply to give 24 and add to give -11.*

*-8 and -3*

> *Write these numbers in the brackets (**x** ± ...)(**x** ± ...).*

$(x-8)(x-3)$

**For ±8 and ±3**** [1] **
**Fully correct**** [1]**

*Write **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* and -5**x** as multiplications of their factors* * *

$x\timesx-5\timesx$ * *

*Factorise the expression (by taking out the common factor of **x**)* * *

$x \left(x - 5\right)$ * *

*This shows that both **x** and **x** - 5 are factors of the whole expression **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* - 5**x*

**x**** - 5** **[1]**

*Method 1*

*Factorise using the difference of two squares, which states that **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2*</sup>* = (**a** + **b**)(**a** - **b**)*

$x^{2} - 8^{2} = \left(x + 8\right) \left(x - 8\right)$

**(****x**** + 8)(****x**** - 8)** **[1]**

*Method 2*

*Expand each of the answers given to see which one is the same as **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* - 64*

$( x + 8 ) ^{2} = ( x + 8 ) ( x + 8 ) = x ^{2} + 16 x + 64$

$\left(x - 8\right)^{2}=\left(x - 8\right) \left(x - 8\right)=x^{2}-16x + 64$

$( x + 8 ) ( x - 8 ) = x^{2} \cancel{+ 8 x} \cancel{- 8 x} - 64 = x^{2} - 64$

$x ( x - 64 ) = x ^{2} - 64 x$

**(****x**** + 8)(****x**** - 8) ****[1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve      $\frac{4x-1}{5}+\frac{x+4}{2}=3$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remove the fractions by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator. *

> *The lowest common denominator is the LCM of 5 and 2 = 10*

$\begin{aligned}10 \left(\frac{4 x - 1}{5}\right) + 10 \left(\frac{x + 4}{2}\right) & = & 10 \left(3\right)\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Simplify by cancelling each fraction. *

> *The fractions should disappear.*

$\begin{aligned}2 \left(4 x - 1\right) + 5 \left(x + 4\right) & = & 30\end{aligned}$

> *Expand both sets of brackets on the left-hand side. *

> *Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}8 x - 2 + 5 x + 20 & = & 30\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify the left hand side by bringing the **x** terms together and the number terms together.*

$\begin{aligned}8 x + 5 x - 2 + 20 & = & 30 \\ 13 x + 18 & = & 30\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract 18 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}13 x & = & 30 - 18 \\ 13 x & = & 12\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 13.*

$x=\frac{12}{13}$

$x=\frac{12}{13}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve   $\frac{5w-8}{3}=4w+2$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remove the fraction by multiplying both sides by 3.*

$\begin{aligned}3 \left(\frac{5 w - 8}{3}\right) & = & 3 \left(4 w + 2\right) \\ 5 w - 8 & = & 3 \left(4 w + 2\right)\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Expand the brackets on the right-hand side. *

> *Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}5 w - 8 & = & 12 w + 6\end{aligned}$

> *Bring the **w** terms to one side by subtracting the term with the smallest coefficient of **w **(**5w**).  *

$\begin{aligned}5 w - 8 & = & 12 w + 6 \\ - 5 w & = & - 5 w \\ - 8 & = & 7 w + 6\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract 6 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}- 8 - 6 & = & 7 w \\ 7 w & = & - 14\end{aligned}$

> *Divide both sides by 7.*

$w=-\frac{14}{7}=-2$

$w=-2$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve    $3 \left(x - 2\right)  =  x + 7$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by expanding the bracket on the left-hand side. Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}3 \left(x - 2\right) & = & x + 7 \\ 3 x - 6 & = & x + 7\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Bring the **x** terms to one side by subtracting the term with the smallest coefficient of **x **(**x**).  *

$\begin{aligned}3 x - 6 & = & x + 7 \\ - x & = & - x \\ 2 x - 6 & = & 7\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Add 6 to both sides.*

$2x=13$

> *Divide both sides by 2.*

$x=\frac{13}{2}=6.5$

$x=6.5$ **[1]**

**Or as a fraction **$\frac{13}{2}$

parts.problemMd: Solve $\frac{2-y}{5}=1$
parts.solutionMd:

$\begin{aligned}5 \left(\frac{2 - y}{5}\right) & = & 5 \left(1\right) \\ 2 - y & = & 5\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Subtract 2 from both sides.*

$-y=5-2\,-y=3$

> *Multiply both sides by -1 to remove the negative sign.*

$y=-3$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve                $\frac{x+1}{3}+\frac{2x+5}{4}=2$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remove the fractions by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator. *

> *The lowest common denominator is the LCM of 3 and 4 = 12*

$\begin{aligned}12 \left(\frac{x + 1}{3}\right) + 12 \left(\frac{2 x + 5}{4}\right) & = & 12 \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Simplify by cancelling each fraction. *

> *The fractions should disappear.*

$\begin{aligned}\cancel{12} \left(\frac{x + 1}{\cancel{3}}\right) + \cancel{ 12} \left(\frac{2 x + 5}{\cancel{4}}\right) & = & 12 \left(2\right) \\ 4 \left(x + 1\right) + 3 \left(2 x + 5\right) & = & 24\end{aligned}$

> *Expand both sets of brackets on the left-hand side. *

> *Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}4 x + 4 + 6 x + 15 & = & 24\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Simplify the left hand side by bringing the **x** terms together and the number terms together.*

$\begin{aligned}4 x + 6 x + 4 + 15 & = & 24 \\ 10 x + 19 & = & 24\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract 19 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}10 x & = & 24 - 19 \\ 10 x & = & 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 10.*

$x=\frac{5}{10}=\frac{1}{2}$

$x=\frac{1}{2}$ **[1] **

**0.5 also accepted**

parts.problemMd: Solve  $\frac{4 \left(8 x  -  2\right)}{3 x}  =  10$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remove the fraction by multiplying both sides by **3x.*

$\begin{aligned}3 x \left(\frac{4 \left(8 x - 2\right)}{3 x}\right) & = & 3 x \left(10\right) \\ 4 \left(8 x - 2\right) & = & 3 x \left(10\right)\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Multiply out the brackets on both sides. *

> *Remember to expand both parts of the bracket on the left.*

$\begin{aligned}32 x - 8 & = & 30 x\end{aligned}$

> *Bring the **x** terms to one side by subtracting the term with the smallest coefficient of **x **(**30x**).  *

$\begin{aligned}32 x - 8 & = & 30 x \\ - 30 x & = & - 30 x \\ 2 x - 8 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Add 8 to both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}2 x & = & 8\end{aligned}$

> *Divide both sides by 2.*

$x=\frac{8}{2}=4$

$x=4$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Simplify     $5x+4y+x-7y$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Collect together the 'like terms' (terms with the same letter) by rearranging the expression. *

> *Remember that you must keep the sign in front of the term when you move it. Be extra careful with the negative term.*

$5x+x+4y-7y$

**[1]**

> *Add/subtract the like terms to simplify the expression.*

$6x-3y$** [1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve $7 \left(x + 2\right)  =  7$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1** *

> *Start by expanding the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}7 \left(x + 2\right) & = & 7 \\ 7 x + 14 & = & 7\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract 14 from both sides.*

$7x=-7$

> *Divide both sides by 7.*

$x=-1$ **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Start by dividing both sides by 7.*

$\begin{aligned}7 \left(x + 2\right) & = & 7 \\ x + 2 & = & 1\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract 2 from both sides.*

$x=1-2$

$x=-1$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve    $\frac{x+2}{3x}+\frac{x-2}{2x}=3$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remove the fractions by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator. *

> *The lowest common denominator is the LCM of 3**x **and 2**x** = 6**x*

$\begin{aligned}6 x \left(\frac{x + 2}{3 x}\right) + 6 x \left(\frac{x - 2}{2 x}\right) & = & 6 x \left(3\right)\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Simplify by cancelling the common terms in each fraction. *

> *The fractions should disappear.*

$\begin{aligned}\cancel{6 x} \left(\frac{x + 2}{\cancel{3 x}}\right) + \cancel{6 x} \left(\frac{x - 2}{\cancel{2 x}}\right) & = & 6 x \left(3\right) \\ 2 \left(x + 2\right) + 3 \left(x - 2\right) & = & 18 x\end{aligned}$

> *Expand both sets of brackets on the left-hand side. *

> *Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}2 x + 4 + 3 x - 6 & = & 18 x\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify the left hand side by bringing the **x** terms together and the number terms together.*

$\begin{aligned}2 x + 3 x + 4 - 6 & = & 18 x \\ 5 x - 2 & = & 18 x\end{aligned}$

> *Bring the **x** terms to one side by subtracting 5**x** from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}- 2 & = & 18 x - 5 x \\ 13 x & = & - 2\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 13.*

$x=\frac{-2}{13}$

$x=-\frac{2}{13}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve         $\frac{15-x}{5}=3x+11$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remove the fraction by multiplying both sides by 5.*

$\begin{aligned}5 \left(\frac{15 - x}{5}\right) & = & 5 \left(3 x + 11\right) \\ 15 - x & = & 5 \left(3 x + 11\right)\end{aligned}$

**15 - x must be correct**** [1]**

> *Expand the brackets on the right-hand side. Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}15 - x & = & 15 x + 55\end{aligned}$

> *Bring the **x** terms to one side by subtracting the term with the smallest coefficient of **x **(**-x**).  *

$\begin{aligned}15 - x & = & 15 x + 55 \\ - \left(- x\right) & = & - \left(- x\right) \\ 15 & = & 16 x + 55\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract 55 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}15 - 55 & = & 16 x \\ 16 x & = & - 40\end{aligned}$

> *Divide both sides by 16.*

$x=\frac{-40}{16}=-\frac{20}{8}=-\frac{5}{2}$

$x=-2.5$**[1] **

**Any equivalent fraction also accepted**

parts.problemMd: Solve    $5x+4=14+x$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Bring the **x** terms to one side by subtracting the term with the smallest coefficient of **x **(**x**).  *

$\begin{aligned}5 x + 4 & = & 14 + x \\ - x & = & - x \\ 4 x + 4 & = & 14\end{aligned}$

parts.problemMd: Solve      $5 \left(f - 3\right)  =  f  +  10$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by expanding the bracket on the left-hand side. Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}5 \left(f - 3\right) & = & f + 10 \\ 5 f - 15 & = & f + 10\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Bring the **f** terms to one side by subtracting the term with the smallest coefficient of **f **(**f)**.  *

$\begin{aligned}5 f - 15 & = & f + 10 \\ - f & = & - f \\ 4 f - 15 & = & 10\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Add 15 to both sides.*

$4x=25$

$f=6.25$ **[1]**

**Or as a fraction **$\frac{25}{4}$

parts.problemMd: Solve   $\frac{h+7}{3}+\frac{2h-1}{2}=\frac{5}{6}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remove the fractions by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator. The lowest common denominator is the LCM of 3 and 2 = 6.*

$\begin{aligned}6 \left(\frac{h + 7}{3}\right) + 6 \left(\frac{2 h - 1}{2}\right) & = & 6 \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Simplify by cancelling each fraction. The fractions should disappear.*

$\begin{aligned}\cancel{6} \left(\frac{h + 7}{\cancel{3}}\right) + \cancel{ 6} \left(\frac{2 h - 1}{\cancel{2}}\right) & = & \cancel{6} \left(\frac{5}{\cancel{6}}\right) \\ 2 \left(h + 7\right) + 3 \left(2 h - 1\right) & = & 5\end{aligned}$

> *Expand both sets of brackets on the left-hand side. Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}2 h + 14 + 6 h - 3 & = & 5\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Simplify the left hand side by bringing the **h** terms together and the number terms together.*

$\begin{aligned}2 h + 6 h + 14 - 3 & = & 5 \\ 8 h + 11 & = & 5\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract 11 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}8 h & = & 5 - 11 \\ 8 h & = & - 6\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 8.*

$h=-\frac{6}{8}=-\frac{3}{4}$

$h=-0.75$ **[1] **

**Any equivalent answer accepted.**

parts.problemMd: Solve      $7 \left(k - 3\right)  =  3 k  - 5$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by expanding the bracket on the left-hand side. Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}7 \left(k - 3\right) & = & 3 k - 5 \\ 7 k - 21 & = & 3 k - 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Bring the **k** terms to one side by subtracting the term with the smallest coefficient of **k **(**3k**).  *

$\begin{aligned}7 k - 21 & = & 3 k - 5 \\ - 3 k & = & - 3 k \\ 4 k - 21 & = & - 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Add 21 to both sides.*

$4k=-5+21\,4k=16$

> *Divide both sides by 4.*

$k=\frac{16}{4}=4$

$k=4$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve       $4 \left(x  +  3\right)  =  2 x  + 8$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by expanding the bracket on the left-hand side. Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}4 \left(x + 3\right) & = & 2 x + 8 \\ 4 x + 12 & = & 2 x + 8\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Bring the **x** terms to one side by subtracting the term with the smallest coefficient of **x **(2**x**).  *

$\begin{aligned}4 x + 12 & = & 2 x + 8 \\ - 2 x & = & - 2 x \\ 2 x + 12 & = & 8\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract 12 from both sides.*

$2x=-4$

> *Divide both sides by 2.*

$x=\frac{-4}{2}=-2$

$x=-2$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve   $\frac{3x-2}{4}-\frac{2x+5}{3}=\frac{1-x}{6}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remove the fractions by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator. *

> *The lowest common denominator is the LCM of 4, 3 and 6 = 12.*

$\begin{aligned}12 \left(\frac{3 x - 2}{4}\right) - 12 \left(\frac{2 x + 5}{3}\right) & = & 12 \left(\frac{1 - x}{6}\right)\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Simplify by cancelling the common terms in each fraction. The fractions should disappear.*

$\begin{aligned}\cancel{12} \left(\frac{3 x - 2}{\cancel{4}}\right) - \cancel{12} \left(\frac{2 x + 5}{\cancel{3}}\right) & = & \cancel{12} \left(\frac{1 - x}{\cancel{6}}\right) \\ 3 \left(3 x - 2\right) - 4 \left(2 x + 5\right) & = & 2 \left(1 - x\right)\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Expand all three sets of brackets. *

> *Remember to expand both parts of the bracket and be careful with the negative sign.*

$\begin{aligned}9 x - 6 - 8 x - 20 & = & 2 - 2 x\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify the left hand side.*

$\begin{aligned}9 x - 8 x - 6 - 20 & = & 2 - 2 x \\ x - 26 & = & 2 - 2 x\end{aligned}$

> *Bring the **x** terms to one side by adding 2**x** to both sides and the number terms to the other by adding 26 to both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}x - 26 & = & 2 - 2 x \\ + 2 x & = & + 2 x \\ 3 x - 26 & = & 2 \\ + 26 & = & + 26 \\ 3 x & = & 28\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 3.*

$x=\frac{28}{3}$

$x=9\frac{1}{3}$ **[1]**

**The improper fraction is also accepted. **

parts.problemMd: Solve        $\frac{11-w}{4}=1+w$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remove the fraction by multiplying both sides by 4.*

$\begin{aligned}4 \left(\frac{11 - w}{4}\right) & = & 4 \left(1 + w\right) \\ 11 - w & = & 4 \left(1 + w\right)\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *Expand the brackets on the right-hand side. *

> *Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}11 - w & = & 4 + 4 w\end{aligned}$

> *Bring the **w** terms to one side by subtracting the term with the smallest coefficient of **w **(-**w**).  *

$\begin{aligned}11 - w & = & 4 + 4 w \\ - \left(- w\right) & = & - \left(- w\right) \\ 11 & = & 4 + 5 w\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract 4 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}11 - 4 & = & 5 w \\ 5 w & = & 7\end{aligned}$

> *Divide both sides by 5.*

$w=\frac{7}{5}$

$w=\frac{7}{5}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve    $5 x  -  6  =  3 \left(x - 1\right)$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by expanding the bracket on the right-hand side. Remember to expand both parts of the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}5 x - 6 & = & 3 \left(x - 1\right) \\ 5 x - 6 & = & 3 x - 3\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Bring the **x** terms to one side by subtracting the term with the smallest coefficient of **x **(3**x**).  *

parts.solutionMd:

> *Although this may at first appear to be a quadratic equations question, it's actually a linear equations question "in disguise"!*

> *Expand the brackets, noting that *$\left(2 x + 5\right)^{2} = \left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x + 5\right)$*.*

$4x^{2}+10x+10x+25=4x^{2}-2x+6x-3$

$4x^{2}+20x+25=4x^{2}+4x-3$

> *Now subtract *$4x^{2}$* from both sides, to reveal the linear equation!*

$\begin{aligned}4 x^{2} + 20 x + 25 & = & 4 x^{2} + 4 x - 3 \\ - 4 x^{2 } & = & - 4 x^{2} \\ 20 x + 25 & = & 4 x - 3\end{aligned}$

> *Solve the linear equation. Subtract *$4x$* from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}16 x + 25 & = & - 3\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract 25 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}16 x & = & - 28\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 16.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{- 28}{16} = - \frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}$

$x=-\frac{7}{4}$ ** [1]**

$x=-\frac{7}{3}\mathrm{and}x=-\frac{11}{3}$** [1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Form an expression for the area of triangle *$T_{1}$* using the formula for the area of a triangle if the perpendicular height is **not **known. *

> *The formula for the area of a triangle is *$A=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the two known sides and *$C$* is the included angle.*

$Area_{T_{1}} = \frac{1}{2} \left(x\right) \left(x\right) sin \left(30 \circ\right)$

**[1]**

> *Form an expression for the area of triangle *$T_{2}$* using the formula for the area of a triangle if the perpendicular height **is **known. The formula for the area of a triangle is *$A=\frac{1}{2}bh$*, where *$b$* is the base and *$h$* is the height perpendicular to the base.*

$Area_{T_{2}} = \frac{1}{2} \left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 1\right)$

**[1]**

> *Use the given information, *$\mathrm{area}T_{1}=\mathrm{area}T_{2}$*, to write an equation in terms of *$x$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \left(x\right) \left(x\right) sin \left(30 \circ\right) & = & \frac{1}{2} \left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 1\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Cancel *$\frac{1}{2}$*, which exists on both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(x\right) \left(x\right) sin \left(30 \circ\right) & = & \left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 1\right) \\ x^{2} sin 30 & = & \left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 1\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Use your knowledge of trig exact values, or your calculator, to evaluate *$sin 30 \circ \left(= \frac{1}{2}\right)$*.*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) & = & \left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 1\right) \\ \frac{1}{2} x^{2 } & = & \left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 1\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Expand the brackets on the RHS of the equation.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} x^{2 } & = & \left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 1\right) \\ \frac{1}{2} x^{2 } & = & x^{2} + x - 2 x - 2 \\ \frac{1}{2} x^{2 } & = & x^{2} - x - 2\end{aligned}$

> *REmove the fraction by multiplying both sides by 2.*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2 } & = & 2 \left(x^{2} - x - 2\right) \\ & = & 2 x^{2} - 2 x - 4\end{aligned}$

> *Rearrange the expression to make a quadratic equation equal to 0.*

$\begin{aligned}0 & = & 2 x^{2} - 2 x - 4 - x^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}2 x^{2} - 2 x - 4 - x^{2} & = & 0 \\ x^{2} - 2 x - 4 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The question asks for the answer to be given in the form *$a+\sqrt{b}$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are integers.*

> * This form can be obtained by either using the quadratic formula, or by completing the square.*

> *Given an equation of the form *$ax^{2}+bx+c=0$*, the quadratic formula is *$x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$*.*

$a=1,b=-2,c=-4$

> *Substitute into the quadratic formula.*

$x = \frac{- \left(- 2\right) \pm \sqrt{\left(- 2\right)^{2} - 4 \times 1 \times \left(- 4\right)}}{2 \times 1}$

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{20}}{2} \\ & = & \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 \times 5}}{2} \\ & = & \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4} \sqrt{5}}{2} \\ & = & \frac{2 \pm 2 \sqrt{5}}{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Cancel out 2 from each term.*

$x = \begin{aligned} & & \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & 1\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & +\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}$* **  or  *$x = \begin{aligned} & & \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & 1\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & -\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}$

> *Considering the diagram in part (a), the lengths of *$T_{1}$* are *$x$*, so *$x$* must be positive. The value *$1-\sqrt{5}$* is negative so this cannot be the length of a triangle. *

** **$x=1+\sqrt{5}$** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Given that $M=$ $\frac{18^{4 n} \times 2^{3 \left(n^{2} - 6 n\right)} \times 3^{2 \left(1 - 4 n\right)}}{12^{2}}$

find the values of $n$ for which $M=2$
parts.solutionMd:
*First we need to rewrite the top as powers of prime numbers only.*

*2 and 3 are already prime, so it is 18 we need to change.* *To do this we need the prime factorisation of 18.*

$\begin{aligned}18 & = & 2 \times 3 \times 3 \\ & = & 2 \times 3^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Rewrite the equation, including substituting in the given value for **M** and multiplying both sides by 12*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$2 \times 12^{2} = \left(2 \times 3^{2}\right)^{4 n} \times 2^{3 \left(n^{2} - 6 n\right)} \times 3^{2 \left(1 - 4 n\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Use the laws of indices *$\left(a b\right)^{m} = a^{m} \times b^{m}$* and *$\left(a^{m}\right)^{n} = a^{m n}$*.*

$288 = 2^{4 n} \times 3^{2 \left(4 n\right)} \times 2^{3 \left(n^{2} - 6 n\right)} \times 3^{2 \left(1 - 4 n\right)}$

> *Use the law of indices *$a^{m}\timesa^{n}=a^{m+n}$* to simplify the right hand side of the equation.*

$288 = 2^{4 n + 3 \left(n^{2} - 6 n\right)} \times 3^{2 \left(4 n\right) + 2 \left(1 - 4 n\right)}$

> *Expand and simplify the powers of 2 and 3.*

$\begin{aligned}288 & = & 2^{4 n + 3 n^{2} - 18 n} \times 3^{8 n + 2 - 8 n} \\ 288 & = & 2^{3 n^{2} - 14 n} \times 3^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *3*<sup>*2*</sup>* is just a number (9) so we can divide both sides by it.  Also simplify the equation.*

$\frac{288}{9}=2^{3n^{2}-14n}\,2^{3n^{2}-14n}=32$

**[1]**

> *Rewriting 32 as a power of 2 allows us to set up an equation by comparing the indices.*

$\begin{aligned}2^{3 n^{2} - 14 n} & = & 2^{5} \\ \therefore 3 n^{2} - 14 n & = & 5 \\ 3 n^{2} - 14 n - 5 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *This is a quadratic and so can be solved either by factorsing, completing the square or using the quadratic formula.*

$3 n^{2} - 14 n - 5 = \left(3 n + 1\right) \left(n - 5\right)$

**[1]**

> *Solve by equating each factor to zero.*

$\begin{aligned}3 n + 1 & = & 0 , n = - \frac{1}{3} \\ n - 5 & = & 0 , n = 5\end{aligned}$

> *There are no restrictions on the values of **n** so both answers are valid.*

$n=-\frac{1}{3},n=5$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
*The value of x will come from (one of) the solutions to *$8x^{2}-6x-275=0$*.*

> *This is a quadratic equation - the easiest way to solve these is, if possible, by factorisation. As "*$a\neq1$*" us the "by grouping" method.*

$\begin{aligned}" a c " & = & - 2200 \\ " b " & = & - 6\end{aligned}$

> *We need a pair of values that multiply to -2200 and add to -6.*

*44 and -50*

> *So rewrite the middle term of the quadratic equation as *$+44x-50x$*.*

$8x^{2}+44x-50x-275=0$

> *Group and factorise the first two terms, then the second two terms.*

$4 x \left(2 x + 11\right) - 25 \left(2 x + 11\right) = 0$

> *There is a factor of *$\left(2 x + 11\right)$* in both terms so this can be factorised further.*

$\left(2 x + 11\right) \left(4 x - 25\right) = 0$

**[2]**

parts.problemMd: Express $7--4x--x^{2}$ in the form $p--(x+q)^{2}$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants.
parts.solutionMd:
*Completing the square is easiest when dealing with a single, positive **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* term, so take a factor of -1.*

> *This is only necessary for the **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* and **x** terms so leave 7 as it is.*

$7 - 4 x - x^{2} = 7 - \left(x^{2} + 4 x\right)$

> *Complete the square for the part in brackets.*

$7 - \left(x^{2} + 4 x\right) = 7 - \left[\left(x + 2\right)^{2} - 4\right]$

**[1]**

> *Expand and rearrange into the required form.*

$\begin{aligned}7 - \left[\left(x + 2\right)^{2} - 4\right] & = & 7 - \left(x + 2\right)^{2} + 4 \\ & = & 11 - \left(x + 2\right)^{2}\end{aligned}$

$\therefore7-4x-x^{2}=11-(x+2)^{2}$ **[1]**

**i.e. **$p=11,q=2$**.**

parts.problemMd:

Find the value of $w$ when $y=10$. Show your working.

parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by substituting *$x=\sqrt{w+1}$* into *$y=6x^{4}+7x^{2}$*.*

$y = 6 \left(\sqrt{w + 1}\right)^{4} + 7 \left(\sqrt{w + 1}\right)^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Expand the brackets, using *$z^{4}=z^{2}z^{2}$* and *$\left(\sqrt{z}\right)^{2} = z$*.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 6 \left(\sqrt{w + 1}\right)^{2} \left(\sqrt{w + 1}\right)^{2} + 7 \left(\sqrt{w + 1}\right)^{2} \\ & = & 6 \left(w + 1\right) \left(w + 1\right) + 7 \left(w + 1\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Continue to expand the brackets.*

$\begin{aligned} & = & 6 \left(w^{2} + 2 w + 1\right) + 7 \left(w + 1\right) \\ & = & 6 w^{2} + 12 w + 6 + 7 w + 7\end{aligned}$

> *And collect like terms.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 6 w^{2} + 19 w + 13\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now substitute *$y=10$* into *$y=6w^{2}+19w+8$*.*

$\begin{aligned}10 & = & 6 w^{2} + 19 w + 13\end{aligned}$

> *Rearrange to the form *$aw^{2}+bw+c=0$* in order to solve.*

$\begin{aligned}6 w^{2} + 19 w + 3 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Solve using factorisation, completing the square, or the quadratic formula. *

> *Here it is relatively easy to find two numbers that multiply to *$ac$* and add to *$b$* so we will use factorisation; but if in doubt, use the quadratic formula!*

$ac=18,b=19,\mathrm{two} \mathrm{numbers} \mathrm{that} \mathrm{multiply} \mathrm{to}ac\mathrm{and} \mathrm{add} \mathrm{to}b\mathrm{are}18\mathrm{and}1$

$\begin{aligned}6 w^{2} + 18 w + 1 w + 3 & = & 0 \\ 6 w \left(w + 3\right) + 1 \left(w + 3\right) & = & 0 \\ \left(w + 3\right) \left(6 w + 1\right) & = & 0\end{aligned}$

**correct factorisation, completing the square or substitution into the quadratic formula ****[1]**

$w=-3$** ***and*** **$w=-\frac{1}{6}$

> *Inspect both solutions to see if they are valid*

$w=-3$* is not a valid solution, as this would lead to a negative square root*

$w=-\frac{1}{6}$** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
$6x^{2}=7xy+20y^{2}$  where  $x>0$ and  $y>0$

Find the ratio  $x:y$
parts.solutionMd:
*Bring all the terms on to one side (for example, to the left-hand side)* * *

$6x^{2}-7xy-20y^{2}=0$

**[1]**

*It's easier here to think about how to factorise with one variable, for example  *$6t^{2}-7t-20$ *Multiply the first and last numbers together* * *

*6 × -20 = -120* * *

*Find two numbers that add to give -7 and multiply to give -120* * *

*-15 and 8* * *

*Split the -7**t** term into -15**t** and 8**t* * *

$6t^{2}-15t+8t-20$ * *

*Factorise the first pair of terms and the second pair of terms* * *

$3 t \left(2 t - 5\right) + 4 \left(2 t - 5\right)$ * *

*The (2**t** - 5) bracket is common in both Factorise this bracket out* * *

$\left(2 t - 5\right) \left(3 t + 4\right)$ * *

*The original expression was  6**x*<sup>*2*</sup>* - 7**xy** - 20**y*<sup>*2*</sup> *To get 6**x*<sup>*2*</sup>* at the beginning and -20**y*<sup>*2*</sup>* at the end, both brackets must start with **x **terms and end with** y** terms* * *

$\left(2 x - 5 y\right) \left(3 x + 4 y\right) = 0$

**[1]**

*Solve this quadratic equation (by solving each bracket equal to zero)* * *

$\begin{aligned}2 x - 5 y & = & 0 \\ 2 x & = & 5 y \\ x & = & \frac{5}{2} y\end{aligned}$*    **or  **  *$\begin{aligned}3 x + 4 y & = & 0 \\ 3 x & = & - 4 y \\ x & = & - \frac{4}{3} y\end{aligned}$ * *

*The ratio **x** : **y** is positive (as **x** > 0 and **y** > 0 in the question) so choose the positive relationship* * *

$x=\frac{5}{2}y$ * *

*Substitute this expression for **x **into the ratio **x** : **y** * * *

> $\begin{aligned}x : y & = & \frac{5}{2} y : y\end{aligned}$*   *

> *Cancel the **y**'s  *

> $\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2} \cancel{y} : \cancel{y} & = & \frac{5}{2} : 1\end{aligned}$*  *

> *Multiply both sides by 2*

**5 : 2*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Triangle $HJK$ is isosceles with $HJ=HK$ and $JK=\sqrt{80}$

$H$ is the point with coordinates $(-4,1)$ 
$J$ is the point with coordinates $(j,15)$ where $j<0$ 
$K$ is the point with coordinates $(6,k)$

$M$is the midpoint of $JK$. 
The gradient of $HM$ is 2

Find the value of $j$and the value of $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use the information *$JK=\sqrt{80}$* to find an equation for the length of the line connecting **J **and **K **in terms of **j **and **k.*

> *The formula for the length between the points (**x*<sub>*1*</sub>*, **y*<sub>*1*</sub>*) and (**x*<sub>*2*</sub>*, **y*<sub>*2*</sub>*) is *$\sqrt{\left(x_{2} - x_{1}\right)^{2} + \left(y_{2} - y_{1}\right)^{2}}$*. Use this formula with the points (**j**, 15) and (6, **k**). *

$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\left(k - 15\right)^{2} + \left(6 - j\right)^{2}} & = & \sqrt{80} \\ \left(k - 15\right)^{2} + \left(6 - j\right)^{2} & = & 80\end{aligned}$

** ****[1]**

> *The line connecting the top vertex of an isosceles triangle (**H**) to the midpoint of its base** **(**JK**) is perpendicular to the base, so the lines **HM **and **JK **are perpendicular.*

> *The** gradients of perpendicular lines are negative reciprocals of each other.*

$m_{JK}=-\frac{1}{m_{HM}}=-\frac{1}{2}$

**[1]**

> *The gradient of **JK **can be found in terms of **j **and **k** and set equal to *$-\frac{1}{2}$*.*

$m_{JK}=\frac{15-k}{j-6}=-\frac{1}{2}$

**[1]**

> *Solve the two equations simultaneously to find the values of **j** and **k. **Number the equations.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(k - 15\right)^{2} + \left(6 - j\right)^{2} & = & 80 \left(1\right) \\ \frac{15 - k}{j - 6} & = & - \frac{1}{2} \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Notice here that the expressions inside the brackets in equation (1) are similar to those on the numerator and denominator of equation (2). Multiply both parts of the fraction by -1 to get the expressions to be the same.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{- \left(15 - k\right)}{- \left(j - 6\right)} & = & - \frac{1}{2} \left(2\right) \\ \frac{k - 15}{6 - j} & = & - \frac{1}{2} \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Rearrange equation (2) to make (**k **-15) the subject.*

$\begin{aligned}k - 15 & = & - \frac{1}{2} \left(6 - j\right) \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute into equation (1).*

$\begin{aligned}\left(- \frac{1}{2} \left(6 - j\right)\right)^{2} + \left(6 - j\right)^{2} & = & 80 \left(1\right) \\ \left(\frac{j}{2} - \frac{6}{2}\right)^{2} + \left(6 - j\right)^{2} & = & 80 \left(1\right) \\ \left(\frac{j}{2} - 3\right)^{2} + \left(6 - j\right)^{2} & = & 80 \left(1\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Expand the brackets and simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{j}{2}\right)^{2} - 6 \left(\frac{j}{2}\right) + 9 + 36 - 12 j + j^{2} & = & 80 \left(1\right) \\ \frac{j^{2}}{4} - 3 j + 45 - 12 j + j^{2} & = & 80 \left(1\right) \\ \frac{5 j^{2}}{4} - 15 j + 45 & = & 80 \left(1\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Rearrange equation (1) to form a quadratic in the form **ax*<sup>*2 *</sup>*+ **bx **+ c = 0*

$\begin{aligned}5 j^{2} - 60 j + 180 & = & 320 \left(1\right) \\ 5 j^{2} - 60 j - 140 & = & 0 \left(1\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Equation (1) can be made easier to solve by dividing every term by 5.*

$\begin{aligned}j^{2} - 12 j - 28 & = & 0 \left(1\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Factorise.*

$( j - 14 ) ( j + 2 ) = 0 ( 1 )$
j space equals space 14 space space space or space space space j space equals space minus 2

**[1]**

> *We are told that **j** < 0, so ignore the positive answer and use the negative value to find the corresponding value of **k** by substituting into equation (2).*

$\begin{aligned}k - 15 & = & - \frac{1}{2} \left(6 - j\right) \left(2\right) \\ k - 15 & = & - \frac{1}{2} \left(6 - \left(- 2\right)\right) \left(2\right) \\ k & = & - \frac{1}{2} \left(8\right) + 15 \left(2\right) \\ k & = & 11\end{aligned}$

$j=-2,k=11$* ***[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
*The midpoint of two coordinates can be thought of as the average (mean) of the two points.* *We can find the mean of the x-coordinates using *$\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2}$* and find the mean of the y-coordinates using *$\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2}$*.*

> *Find an expression in terms of **b **for the midpoint of **AB.*

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}\frac{- 3 + 47}{2} & = & a \\ \frac{44}{2} & = & a \\ a & = & 22\end{aligned}$

> *Use the **y **coordinate to form and solve an equation in terms of *$b$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{11 + b}{2} & = & - 19 \\ 11 + b & = & - 38 \\ b & = & - 38 - 11\end{aligned}$

$a=22,b=-49$** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$A$ and $B$ are straight lines.

Line $A$ has equation $2y=3x+8$ 
Line $B$ goes through the points $(---1,2)$ and $(2,8)$

Do lines $A$ and $B$ intersect? 
You must show all your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Two straight lines will always intersect unless they are parallel Parallel lines have the same gradients so find the gradient of both lines*

> *We can find the gradient of Line **A** ** by rearranging into the form *$y=mx+c$

$\begin{aligned}2 y & = & 3 x + 8 \\ y & = & \frac{3}{2} x + 4\end{aligned}$

> *Therefore Line **A** has a gradient of *$\frac{3}{2}$

**[1]**

> *Next we can find the gradient of Line **B**, using the gradient formula *$\frac{y_{1}-y_{2}}{x_{1}-x_{2}}$*, taking *$\left(- 1 , 2\right)$* **as *$\left(x_{1} ,  y_{1}\right)$* and *$\left(2 , 8\right)$* as *$\left(x_{2} ,  y_{2}\right)$

$\frac{2-8}{-1-2}=\frac{-6}{-3}=2$

> *Therefore Line **B** has a gradient of 2, which is not the same gradient as line **A*

**Line A and Line B must intersect as they are not parallel ****[1]**

**It is possible to answer this question by working out the equation of Lines A and B in the form **$y=mx+c$** and then equating them to see if there is a solution. But the method presented here is much more efficient!**

> *For **AB **use the formula with the points (-4, -2) and (1, 10). Use brackets around negatives.*

**65 cm ****[1]**

The gradient of the line is 2

parts.solutionMd:
> *Let **P ** have the coordinates **x **and **y.*

> *Form an equation in terms of **x **and **y **for the gradient of **P, **using the formula for the gradient, *$\text{gradient}=\frac{\text{change in}y}{\text{change in}x}=\frac{y_{2}-y_{1}}{x_{2}-x_{1}}$*.*

$2=\frac{y-(0)}{x-0}=\frac{y}{x}$

> *Rearrange to find an expression for **y **in terms of **x.*

$y=2x$

** [1]**

> *Substitute into the formula for the length of a line segment, *$d = \sqrt{\left(x_{2} - x_{1}\right)^{2} + \left(y_{2} - y_{1}\right)^{2}} .$

$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\left(x - 0\right)^{2} + \left(2 x - 0\right)^{2}} & = & \sqrt{2645} \\ \left(x\right)^{2} + \left(2 x\right)^{2} & = & 2645 \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} + 4 x^{2} & = & 2645 \\ 5 x^{2} & = & 2645 \end{aligned}$

> *Divide both sides by 5.*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} & = & \frac{2645}{5} = 529\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Square root both sides to find **x**.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & 23\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute in to the original equation to find **y.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 2 x = 2 \left(23\right) = 46\end{aligned}$

$P(23,46)$ **[1]**

> *For demonstration purposes, we will add the points E, F and G to the diagram below.*

$\mathrm{BG}=12-9=3$

![gcse-ocr-tqs-coordinate-geometry-h2-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/graphs-and-coordinates/coordinate-geometry/assets/003-gcse-ocr-tqs-coordinate-geometry-h2-2.png)

> * And (from the diagram):*

$\begin{aligned}13 & = & 3 + 3 + FG \end{aligned}$

> *We can use this to find FG.*

$\begin{aligned}13 & = & 6 + FG \\ FG & = & 7\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *FG = DF = GC because all the triangles are congruent. If we like we can add these lengths to the diagram. *

> *C has the same **y-**coordinate as A but we need to add 3 + 3 + 3 + 7 to the **x**-coordinate. *

$\begin{aligned}C & = & \left(\left[4 + 3 + 3 + 7 + 7\right] , 9\right) \\ & = & \left(24 , 9\right)\end{aligned}$

**Final answer:** $C=(24,9)$** **

**correct x-coordinate**** [1] **

$\begin{aligned}D & = & \left(\left[4 + 3 + 3\right] , \left[9 - 7\right]\right) \\ & = & \left(10 , 2\right)\end{aligned}$

**Final answer:** $D=(10,2)$** **

parts.problemMd:
A straight line goes through the points ($p,q$) and ($r,s$), where

- $p+2=r$
- $q+4=s.$

Find the gradient of the line.
parts.solutionMd:
> *If *$r=p+2$* and *$s=q+4$* then we can rewrite *$\left(r , s\right)$* in terms of *$p$* and *$q$*.*

$\left(r , s\right) = \left(p + 2 , q + 4\right)$

> *Now we can substitute into the gradient formula *$\frac{y_{1}-y_{2}}{x_{1}-x_{2}}$*, taking *$\left(p + 2 , q + 4\right)$* **as *$\left(x_{1} ,  y_{1}\right)$* and *$\left(p ,  q\right)$* as *$\left(x_{2} ,  y_{2}\right)$*.*

$m=\frac{q+4-q}{p+2-p}$

**[1]**

> *Collecting like terms cancels out the *$p$*s and *$q$*s in the denominator and numerator so that;*

$m=\frac{4}{2}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify *$\frac{4}{2}$* to 2.*

**The gradient of the line is 2 ****[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for the area of a triangle is *$A=\frac{1}{2}bh$* where *$b$* is the base and *$h$* is the height.*

![hLslfHjw_gcse-aqa-tq-coordinate-geomtery-m-q6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/graphs-and-coordinates/coordinate-geometry/assets/022-hlslfhjw-gcse-aqa-tq-coordinate-geomtery-m-q6.png)

> *To find the distance apart the coordinates should be, set the formula equal to 28 square units and solve to find the product of the base and the height. *

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} b h & = & 28 \\ b h & = & 56\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Choose coordinates such that the distance from (0, 0) to (**c, **0) multiplied by the distance from (0, **a**) to (0, **b**) equals 56.*

> *Find a factor pair of 56 that is easy to work with, for example 7 and 8.*

> *Choosing the height to be 7, then **c **= 7 and the distance from (0, **a**) to (0, **b**) needs to be 8, with **a **positive and **b **negative. Choosing **a **= 5 and the distance from (0, **a**) to (0, **b**) needs to be 8, with **a **positive and **b **negative, so **b **will be -3.*

parts.problemMd: Write $3x^{2}-12x+7$ in the form $a(x+b)^{2}+c$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for completing the square for a quadratic in the form*$ax^{2}+bx+c$* is *$a \left(x + \frac{b}{2 a}\right)^{2} - \frac{b^{2}}{4 a} + c$*. *

> *Applying this formula gives*

$3 x^{2} - 12 x + 7 = 3 \left(x + \frac{- 12}{2 \times 3}\right)^{2} - \frac{\left(- 12\right)^{2}}{4 \times 3} + 7$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}3 x^{2} - 12 x + 7 & = & 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 12 + 7 \\ & = & 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**
** **$\therefore 3 \mathbf{\mathit{x}}^{2} - 12 \mathbf{\mathit{x}} + 7 = 3 \left(\mathbf{\mathit{x}} - 2\right)^{2} - 5$* ***[1]**

**i.e.  **$a=3,b=-2,c=-5$**.**

parts.problemMd: Express $7+12x--3x^{2}$ in the form $a+b(x+c)^{2}$ where $a,b$ and$c$are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *The formula for completing the square for a quadratic in the form*$ax^{2}+bx+c$* is *$a \left(x + \frac{b}{2 a}\right)^{2} - \frac{b^{2}}{4 a} + c$*.*

> *Rearrange *$7+12x-3x^{2}$* into the form *$ax^{2}+bx+c.$

$7+12x-3x^{2}=-3x^{2}+12x+7$

> *Therefore *$a=-3,b=12\mathrm{and}c=7$*.*

> *Applying the formula gives*

$- 3 x^{2} + 12 x + 7 = - 3 \left(x + \frac{12}{2 \times - 3}\right)^{2} - \frac{\left(12\right)^{2}}{4 \times - 3} + 7$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}- 3 x^{2} + 12 x + 7 & = & - 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 12 + 7 \\ & = & - 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 19\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange into the format required.*

$19 - 3 \left(\mathbf{\mathit{x}} - 2\right)^{2}$* ***[1]**

** i.e.  **$a=19,b=-3,c=-2$**.**

> *Method 2*

> *Expand the given expression in terms of *$a,b\mathrm{and}c.$

$a + b \left(x + c\right)^{2} = a + b \left(x^{2} + 2 c x + c^{2}\right)$

> *Simplify.*

$a + b \left(x + c\right)^{2} = a + b x^{2} + 2 b c x + b c^{2}$

> *Therefore *$7+12x-3x^{2}=a+bx^{2}+2bcx+bc^{2}$*.*

> *Equating the *$x^{2}$* term gives*

$-3x^{2}=bx^{2}\thereforeb=-3$

**[1]**

> *Equating the *$x$* term gives*

$12x=2bcx$

> *Substitute *$b=-3$*.*

$\begin{aligned}12 x & = & 2 \left(- 3\right) c x \\ 12 & = & - 6 c \\ c & = & - 2\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Equating the constant terms gives*

$7=a+bc^{2}$

> *Substitute *$b=-3$* and *$c=-2$*.*

$\begin{aligned}7 & = & a + \left(- 3\right) \left(- 2\right)^{2} \\ 7 & = & a + \left(- 12\right) \\ a & = & 7 + 12 \\ a & = & 19\end{aligned}$

> *Rearrange into the format required.*

$19 - 3 \left(\mathbf{\mathit{x}} - 2\right)^{2}$* ***[1]**

** i.e.  **$a=19,b=-3,c=2$**.**

parts.solutionMd:
> **[exam-tip]**
> The question refers to 'exact' coordinates of any points of intersection with the coordinate axes.
> 
> This is a hint that $x^{2}--6x+4=0$  is unlikely to be solvable by factorising. Therefore, either completing the square or the quadratic formula should be used.
> 
> As the completed square form is also a way to find the coordinates of the turning point, it is more efficient here to use this method for both the turning point and the roots.

> *The coordinates of the turning point are found by writing the function in completed square form (*$\left(x - a\right)^{2} + b$*, where *$\left(a ,  b\right)$* are the coordinates of the turning point)*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} - 6 x + 4 & = & \left(x - 3\right)^{2} - 9 + 4 \\ & = & \left(x - 3\right)^{2} - 5\end{aligned}$

**[M1 A1]**

*The coordinates of the turning point are (3, -5)*

> *The roots of the function (the intersection with **x**-axis) occur when *$y=0$

> *Therefore you can solve the equation for **x** using the completed square form*

$\begin{aligned}\left(x - 3\right)^{2} - 5 & = & 0 \\ \left(x - 3\right)^{2} & = & 5 \\ x - 3 & = & \pm \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}$

$x=3+\sqrt{5}$* or *$x=3-\sqrt{5}$

**[M1 A1]**

*The coordinates of the intersections with the ***x***-axis are *$\left(3 - \sqrt{5} , 0\right)$* and *$\left(3 + \sqrt{5} , 0\right)$

> *The y-intercept can be found by substituting *$x=0$* into the function*

$\left(0\right)^{2} - 6 \left(0\right) + 4 = 4$

*The y-intercept is (0, 4)*

> *Make a sketch of the curve, C, labelling the coordinates of the intersections with the axes and the coordinates of the turning point as below*

![Graph of a quadratic function with a vertex at (3, -5) and intercepts at (3-√5, 0), (3+√5, 0), and (0, 4), showing axes and curve.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/graphs-and-coordinates/graphs-of-functions/assets/005-graph-of-a-quadratic-function-with-a-vertex-at-3.png)

**[B1 B1]**

> 
> **A1**: For calculating the* x*-coordinate of the turning point correctly. This mark will still be awarded for an incorrectly evaluated *x*-coordinate of the turning point as long as the first M1 mark has been awarded.
> 
> **M1**: Showing a  correct method for calculating the roots of the equation will gain this mark (e.g. substituting correctly into the quadratic formula or completing the square).
> 
> **A1**: This mark is awarded for the two exact solutions of the roots of the equations calculated in any equivalent form (e.g. $x=3\pm\sqrt{5}$)

> *Calculate the gradient between the two points by substituting the given coordinates into the formula *$m = \frac{\left(y_{2} - y_{1}\right)}{\left(x_{2} - x_{1}\right)}$* *

$\begin{aligned}y + 1 & = & \frac{8}{3} x - \frac{8}{3} \\ y & = & \frac{8}{3} x - \frac{8}{3} - 1 \\ y & = & \frac{8}{3} x - \frac{11}{3}\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Start by multiplying both sides by 3 to get rid of the fractions*

$\begin{aligned}3 y & = & 8 x - 11 \\ 0 & = & 8 x - 3 y - 11 \\ 11 & = & 8 x - 3 y\end{aligned}$

$8x-3y=11$

**[A1]**

> *Find the gradient **PQ **in terms of *$a$* and *$b$*using** ** *$m=\frac{y_{1}-y_{2}}{x_{1}-x_{2}}$*, taking **P **as *$\left(x_{1} ,  y_{1}\right)$* and **Q** as *$\left(x_{2} ,  y_{2}\right)$

$m=\frac{4-b}{3-a}$

**[1]**

> *We need to find a value for *$m$* to equate this to and rearrange to "*$b=...$*" (*$b$* in terms of *$a$*) *

> *Find the gradient of the line perpendicular to **PQ **by rearranging it to the form *$y=mx+c$

$\begin{aligned}2 y & = & - 3 x + 7 \\ y & = & - \frac{3}{2} x + \frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Therefore the gradient of the line perpendicular to **PQ** is *$-\frac{3}{2}$*. Gradients of perpendicular lines are negative reciprocals so*

*gradient of ***PQ*** *$\begin{aligned} & = & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Equate the two forms of *$m$* found*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & = & \frac{4 - b}{3 - a}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Cross multiply to clear the fractions*

$\begin{aligned}2 \left(3 - a\right) & = & 3 \left(4 - b\right)\end{aligned}$

**any sensible sketch ****[1]**

> *The gradient of **AB** using the gradient formula, *$m=\frac{y_{1}-y_{2}}{x_{1}-x_{2}}$*, is*

$m_{AB}=\frac{1-5}{-2-6}=\frac{1}{2}$

> *AB **and **BC** are perpendicular therefore their gradients are negative reciprocals therefore*

$m_{BC}=-2$

**[1]**

> *Now we can substitute *$m=-2$*, *$\left(6 , 5\right)$* and *$\left(4 , k\right)$* into the gradient formula for **BC **and solve to find *$k$

$\begin{aligned}- 2 & = & \frac{5 - k}{6 - 4} \\ - 2 & = & \frac{5 - k}{2} \\ - 4 & = & 5 - k \\ k & = & 9\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Now we know that *$C$* is *$\left(4 , 9\right)$* and we can find the equation of a line through *$A \left(- 2 , 1\right)$* and *$C \left(4 , 9\right)$ *First find the gradient*

$\begin{aligned}9 & = & \frac{4}{3} \left(4\right) + c \\ 9 & = & \frac{16}{3} + c \\ c & = & \frac{11}{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Finally we can rearrange into the form *$ay+bx=c$*. Start by multiplying all terms by 3 to clear the fractions, then collect the terms in *$x$* and *$y$* on the left hand side*

$\begin{aligned}3 y & = & 4 x + 11 \\ 3 y - 4 x & = & 11\end{aligned}$

parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the coordinates of **M** (the midpoint of **BC** ) using the formula for the midpoint of two coordinates, *$M = \left(\frac{x_{1} + x_{2}}{2} , \frac{y_{1} + y_{2}}{2}\right)$*.*

$\begin{aligned}M & = & \left(\frac{- 1 + 2}{2} , \frac{5 + 10}{2}\right) = \left(\frac{1}{2} , \frac{15}{2}\right) = \left(0 . 5 , 7 . 5\right)\end{aligned}$

** ****[1]**

> *The line connecting the top vertex of an isosceles triangle (**A**) to the midpoint of its base** **(**BC**) is perpendicular to the base, so the lines **AM **and **BC **are perpendicular. *

> *A diagram will help to see this. *

> *Find the gradient of **BC** using the formula for the gradient of a line connecting two coordinates, *$m = \left( \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}\right)$*, and the points **B **and **C.*

$m_{B C} = \frac{10 - 5}{2 - \left(- 1\right)} = \frac{5}{3}$

**[1]**

> *Find the gradient of **AM** using the fact that the lines are perpendicular so *$m_{AM}=-\frac{1}{m_{BC}}$*.*

$m_{AM}=-\frac{1}{m_{BC}}=-\frac{1}{\frac{5}{3}}=-\frac{3}{5}$

**[1]**

> *The coordinate **M **(0.5, 7.5) is on the line **AM** **so the equation of the straight line **AM** can be found by substituting *$m=-\frac{3}{5}$* and (0.5, 7.5)  into **y **= **mx **+ **c.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & - \frac{3}{5} x + c \\ \left(7 . 5\right) & = & - \frac{3}{5} \left(0 . 5\right) + c\end{aligned}$

** [1]**

> *Rearrange to find **c.*

$7.5=-\frac{3}{10}+c\,c=7.5+\frac{3}{10}=\frac{39}{5}$

> *Substitute the gradient (**m**) **and** the value of **c** into the equation **y **= **mx **+ **c.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & - \frac{3}{5} x + \frac{39}{5}\end{aligned}$

> *Get rid of the fractions by multiplying everything through by 5.*

$\begin{aligned}5 y & = & - 3 x + 39\end{aligned}$

> *Rearrange into the required format by adding 3**x **to both sides**.*

$\begin{aligned}5 y + 3 x & = & 39\end{aligned}$

$5y+3x=39$* ***[1]**

$\begin{aligned}m_{A B} & = & \frac{3 - 2}{5 - \left(- 6\right)} \\ & = & \frac{1}{11}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Perpendicular gradients are negative reciprocals so from this we can deduce the gradient of **CM** .*

$\begin{aligned}m_{C M} & = & - 1 \div \frac{1}{11} \\ & = & - 11\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now find the equation of **CM** by substituting the point *$M \begin{aligned} & & \left(- \frac{1}{2} , \frac{5}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$* and the gradient *$-11$* into *$y=mx+c$*, and solving for **c**.*

> * *$\begin{aligned}y & = & m x + c \\ \frac{5}{2} & = & - 11 \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right) + c \\ \frac{5}{2} & = & \frac{11}{2} + c \\ \frac{5 - 11}{2} & = & c \\ c & = & \frac{- 6}{2} = - 3\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now we know that the equation of **CM** is:*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & - 11 x - 3\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute *$x=-1$* into the equation of **CM** to find the **y**-coordinate of **C.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & - 11 \left(- 1\right) + 3 \\ & = & 11 - 3 \\ & = & 8\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now we can find the length of **CM** using the length of a line segment formula, *$length = \sqrt{\left(x_{1} - x_{2}\right)^{2} + \left(y_{1} - y_{2}\right)^{2}}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}C M & = & \sqrt{\left(- \frac{1}{2} - \left(- 1\right)\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{5}{2} - 8\right)^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{11}{2}\right)^{2}} \\ & = & \frac{\sqrt{122}}{2}\end{aligned}$

> *And finding the length of **AB** is straightforward as we already have the coordinates of **A **and** B.*

$\begin{aligned}A B & = & \sqrt{\left(3 - 2\right)^{2} + \left(5 - \left(- 6\right)\right)^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{122}\end{aligned}$

**length of CM and AB**** ****found**** [1]**

> *Finally, we are ready to find the area of triangle **ABC** using area of a triangle = *$\frac{1}{2}$*× base × height.*

$\mathrm{Area}=\frac{1}{2}\times\sqrt{122}\times\frac{\sqrt{122}}{2}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned} & = & \frac{122}{4} \\ & = & \frac{61}{2}\end{aligned}$

$\mathrm{Area}=30.5\mathrm{units}^{2}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Line A has equation $y=4x--1$

Line B is

perpendicular to line A 
and 
passes through the point (8, 5)

Work out the coordinates of the point where line B intersects the $x$-axis.
parts.solutionMd:
> *From *$y=mx+c$*, Line A has gradient 4. The gradients of perpendicular lines are negative reciprocals so the gradient of the line perpendicular to Line A** **is;*

$m=-1\div4=-\frac{1}{4}$

**[1]**

> *Line B therefore takes the form *$y=-\frac{1}{4}x+c$* and passes through *$\left(8 , 5\right)$*. Substitute this point into the equation.*

$5 = - \frac{1}{4} \left(8\right) + c$

**[1]**

> *Solve for *$c$*.*

$\begin{aligned}5 & = & - 2 + c \\ 7 & = & c\end{aligned}$

> *Now we can write the equation of Line B in the form *$y=mx+c$*.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & - \frac{1}{4} x + 7\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute *$y=0$* into Line B and solve for *$x$* to find where it intersects the *$x$*-axis.*

$\begin{aligned}0 & = & - \frac{1}{4} x + 7\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *(Subtract 7 from both sides)*

$\begin{aligned}- 7 & = & - \frac{1}{4} x\end{aligned}$

> *(Multiply both sides by -4)*

$\begin{aligned}28 & = & x\end{aligned}$

> *Write the final answer as a pair of coordinates.*

$(28,0)$ **[1]**

> *In a **speed-time graph**, the **area under the graph** is the **distance**.*

![aqa-gcse-real-life-graphs-h6-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/graphs-and-coordinates/real-life-graphs/assets/019-aqa-gcse-real-life-graphs-h6-1.png)

*area of triangle*$=\frac{1}{2}\times4\times10$

**[1]**

*   = 20*

> *The distance remaining to reach 75 metres is;*

*75 − 20 = 55 metres*

> *From 4 seconds onwards, the graph is a rectangle so area = length × height. The area needed is 55, the height is 10 and we need the length marked *$x$* on the diagram that gives 55. (Note that although it's marked on the diagram between 9 and 10, this is a guess and we don't actually know yet where it will be). *

$\begin{aligned}55 & = & x \times 10 \\ x & = & \frac{55}{10} = 5 . 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *So the total time to reach 75 metres is the first 4 seconds plus another 5.5 seconds. *

*total time = 4 + 5.5 = 9.5 seconds*

**9.5 seconds** **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *In a **speed-time graph**, the **area under the graph** is the **distance.*

> *This graph is in the shape of a trapezium and area of a trapezium *$= \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) \times h$* where *$a$* and *$b$* are the parallel lines and *$h$* is the height.*

![aqa-gcse-real-life-graphs-h6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/graphs-and-coordinates/real-life-graphs/assets/020-aqa-gcse-real-life-graphs-h6.png)

$t$* ***and*** '*$t-4$**'  or equivalent ****[1]**

> *In the diagram above, the longer parallel length has been called *$t$*. Note that although it's marked on the diagram between 10 and 11, we don't actually know yet where it will be- it's marked on the diagram for demonstration purposes only. The trick to this question is to find the value of *$t$* that gives an area of 75.*

> *The smaller parallel length becomes  *$t-4$* and the height , *$h$*, is 10. Substitute these into the trapezium formula and equate to 75.*

$75 = \frac{1}{2} \left(t + t - 4\right) \times 10$

**[1]**

> *Solve for *$t$*.*

$\begin{aligned}75 & = & 5 \left(2 t - 4\right) \\ \div 5 & = & \div 5 \\ 15 & = & 2 t - 4 \\ + 4 & = & + 4 \\ 19 & = & 2 t \\ \div 2 & = & \div 2 \\ 9 . 5 & = & t\end{aligned}$

**After 9.5 seconds*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Bottles of drink are for sale at three shops.

The normal price of a bottle is the same at each shop.

![q18-paper1h-june2017-aqa-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/number/exchange-rates-and-best-buys/assets/001-q18-paper1h-june2017-aqa-gcse-maths.png)

What is the cheapest way to buy **exactly **8 bottles?

You can buy from more than one shop.

You **must **show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Consider buying exactly 8 bottles in each shop separately. Imagine each bottle costs £1.*

> *Shop A sells 2 at half price for every 1 full price bottle bought, so it makes sense to consider buying these bottles in groups of 3. You could either buy 3 or 6 bottle from shop A. *

Shop space straight A colon
$3 bottles = 1 \times £ 1 + 2 \times £ 0.50 = £ 2$
$6 bottles = 2 \times £ 1 + 4 \times £ 0.50 = £ 4$

> *Shop B sells 3 at half price for every 2 full price bottles bought, so it makes sense to consider buying these bottles in groups of 5. You could buy 5 bottles from shop B. *

Shop space straight B colon space
$5 bottles = 2 \times £ 1 + 3 \times £ 0.50 = £ 3.50$

> *Shop C sells every bottle at 30% off, so you could buy any number of the bottles at 30% off the full price.*

> *Consider the different options. *

> *Option 1: Buy all 8 at shop C.*

> *To buy something at 30% off the price, you still need to pay 70% of the original price, so the easiest way to take 30% off of £1 is to multiply is by 0.7.*

Shop space straight C colon space
$8 bottles = 8 \times £ 1 \times 0.7 = £ 5.60$

** ****Any of the above ****[1]**

> *Looking at the other shops you can see that buying 5 bottles from shop B and 3 from shop A is less than this, so this is a better option.*

> *Option 2: Buy 5 from shop B and 3 from shop A.*

$Shop A \left(3 bottles\right) and shop B \left(5 bottles\right) = \pounds 2 + \pounds 3 . 50 = \pounds 5 . 50$

> *The third option is buying 6 from shop A, but then you could not benefit from the offer at shop B, so you could buy the other 2 from shop C at 30% off.*

> * *$Shop A \left(6 bottles\right) and shop C \left(2 bottles\right) = \pounds 4 + \left(2 \times \pounds 1 \times 0 . 7\right) = \pounds 4 + \pounds 1 . 4 0 = \pounds 5 . 40$

**Any combination found ****[1]**

**The cheapest option is to buy 6 bottles from shop A and 2 from shop C. ****[1]**

parts.problemMd: Show that      $a \% of b = b \% of a$
parts.solutionMd:
*In general to find a percentage of a number, we use a multiplier* *e.g. to find 23% of 100 we would find 0.23 × 100* *0.23 is 23 divided by 100*

> *So in general to find **a**% of **b*

$a \% o f b = \frac{a}{100} \times b = \frac{1}{100} \times a \times b$

> *To find **b**% of **a*

$a\times\frac{b}{100}=\frac{1}{100}\timesa\timesb$

**These two statements are identical, therefore ****a****% of ****b**** is the same as ****b****% of ****a** **[1]** 
**Full, clear, working must be shown for this question**

parts.problemMd:
Josh buys and sells books for a living.

He buys 120 books for £4 each.

He sells $\frac{1}{2}$  of the books for £5 each.

He sells 40% of the books for £7 each. 
He sells the rest of the books for £8 each.

Calculate Josh’s percentage profit.
parts.solutionMd:
> *120 books are bought for £4 each*

*120 × £4 = £480 spent*

**[1]**

> $\frac{1}{2}$* of the books are sold for £5 each*

$\frac{1}{2}\times120=60$* books* 
*60 × £5 = £300 income*

**Income for at least one of the selling prices ****[1]**

> *40% are sold for £7 each*

*0.4 × 120 = 48 books* 
*48 × £7 = £336 income*

> *The rest are sold for £8 each*

$\frac{1}{2}$* (50%) were sold at £5, and 40% were sold at £7, which adds up to 90%. So 10% remain* 
*0.1 × 120 = 12 books* 
*12 × £8 = £96 income*

> *Find the total income*

*£300 + £336 + £96 = £732*

**Method to find total income ****[1]**

> *Find the percentage profit using *$\frac{\mathrm{Income}-\mathrm{Amount} \mathrm{Spent}}{\mathrm{Amount} \mathrm{Spent}}\times100$

$\frac{732 - 480}{480} \times 100 = 52 . 5 \%$

**Method to find percentage profit ****[1]**

**52.5%** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
James is taking three examination papers in Spanish. Here are his first two results.

Paper 1:   $\frac{43}{80}$         Paper 2:   $\frac{38}{65}$

Paper 3 is out of 95. 
The marks in each of the three papers are added together.

Find the lowest mark that James needs in Paper 3 to achieve 60% of the total marks.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The total of James' marks is the sum of the numerators for Paper 1 and Paper 2, plus *$x$* if we let *$x$* be his Paper 3 mark.*

*James' total mark*$=43+38+x=81+x$

> *The total marks available in all three papers is the sum of the denominators for Papers 1 and 2, plus 95.*

*Total marks available = 80 + 65 + 95 = 240*

**[1]**

> *The percentage of the three papers is James' total mark (*$81+x$*) over the the total marks available (240). Make an equation equating this to 60% (60% is 0.6).*

$\frac{81+x}{240}=0.6$

> *Solve. Start by multiplying both sides by 240 to clear the fraction.*

$81+x=240\times0.6\,81+x=144$

**[1]**

> *Subtract 81 from both sides.*

$x=144-81$

**[1]**

**Answer = 63 marks** **[1]**

> *Turn the division into a multiplication Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal*

parts.problemMd:
Each month Edna spends all her income on rent, on travel and on other living expenses.

She spends $\frac{1}{3}$ of her income on rent.

She spends $\frac{1}{5}$ of her income on travel.

She spends `$ 420` of her income on other living expenses.

Work out her income each month.
parts.solutionMd:
> *We can find the total portion of Edna's income spent on rent and travel*

$\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{5}$

> *Use a common denominator of 15 to add the fractions*

$\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{5}=\frac{1\times5}{3\times5}+\frac{1\times3}{5\times3}=\frac{5}{15}+\frac{3}{15}=\frac{8}{15}$

**[1]**

> *This means that *$\frac{8}{15}$* of her income is spent on rent and travel, and we can then find the remaining portion which is spent on other living expenses*

$1-\frac{8}{15}=\frac{7}{15}$* spent on other living expenses*

**[1]**

> *We are told that \$420 is spent on other living expenses, and we know this represents *$\frac{7}{15}$* of Edna's income*

$Income \times \frac{7}{15} = \$ 420$

**Method to find income, working backwards from 7/15 ****[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 15, and then divide both sides by 7 to find her income*

$\begin{aligned}Income \times 7 & = & \$ 6300 \\ Income & = & \$ 900\end{aligned}$

**\$900** **[1]**

*Convert the mixed numbers to improper fractions.* 
*Use the fact that *$3=\frac{12}{4}$* and *$2=\frac{6}{3}$*.*

$3\frac{1}{4}=\frac{12}{4}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{13}{4}\,2\frac{2}{3}=\frac{6}{3}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{8}{3}$

> *To subtract fractions you need a common denominator. 12 is the lowest common multiple of 4 and 3. *
*Convert both fractions so that they have a denominator of 12 by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same value.*

$\frac{13}{4}\times\frac{3}{3}=\frac{39}{12}\,\frac{8}{3}\times\frac{4}{4}=\frac{32}{12}$

**[1]**

> *Once the denominators are the same, you can then subtract the numerators.*

$\frac{39}{12}-\frac{32}{12}=\frac{39-32}{12}$

**[1]**

> *Although the question said "without using a calculator", you should still use your calculator to check your answer.*

$\frac{7}{12}$ **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Subtract the whole numbers and the fractions separately.*

$3-2=1$

> *To subtract fractions you need a common denominator. 12 is the lowest common multiple of 4 and 3. *
*Convert both fractions so that they have a denominator of 12 by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same value.*

$\frac{1}{4}\times\frac{3}{3}=\frac{3}{12}\,\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{4}{4}=\frac{8}{12}$

**[1]**

> *Once the denominators are the same, you can then subtract the numerators.*

$\frac{3}{12}-\frac{8}{12}=-\frac{5}{12}$

> *Combine the whole number and fraction.*

$1-\frac{5}{12}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract by converting the whole number to a fraction. Use the fact that *$1=\frac{12}{12}$*.*

$1-\frac{5}{12}=\frac{12}{12}-\frac{5}{12}=\frac{7}{12}$

> *Although the question said "without using a calculator", you should still use your calculator to check your answer.*

$\frac{7}{12}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A unit fraction has a numerator equal to 1, for example $\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{7}$ and $\frac{1}{25}$.

Unit fractions can be written as the sum of two different unit fractions, for example

$\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{6}$

Write each of the following unit fractions as the sum of two **different** unit fractions.

`1 fourth space equals space 1 over square space plus space 1 over square`

`1 fifth space equals space 1 over square space plus space 1 over square`

`1 over 6 space equals space 1 over square space plus space 1 over square`
parts.solutionMd:
> *For the first equation, pick a fraction which is less that *$\frac{1}{4}$* and call the other **a*

$\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{5}+a$

> *Subtract *$\frac{1}{5}$* from both sides to find **a*

$\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{5}=a\,\frac{1\times5}{4\times5}-\frac{1\times4}{5\times4}=\frac{5}{20}-\frac{4}{20}=\frac{1}{20}=a$

> *So the first equation can be written as *

$\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{20}$ **[1]**

> *We can use the same process for the next two equations*

$\frac{1}{5}=\frac{1}{6}+b\,\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{6}=b\,\frac{6}{30}-\frac{5}{30}=\frac{1}{30}=b$

$\frac{1}{5}=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{30}$ **[1]**

$\frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{7}+c\,\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{7}=c\,\frac{7}{42}-\frac{6}{42}=\frac{1}{42}=c$

$\frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{7}+\frac{1}{42}$** ****[1]**

**There are many solutions to this question which satisfy the equations, and any correct sum, provided they are unit fractions, will have the full marks awarded** 
**You could use your calculator to check your answers**

> *Convert the improper fraction back to a mixed number. *

$1\frac{23}{24}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Write $\left(\sqrt[4]{8}\right)^{5}$ as a power of 2.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Rewrite 8 as 2*<sup>*3*</sup>

$\left(\sqrt[4]{2^{3}}\right)^{5}$

**[1]**

> *A fourth-root, *`fourth root of blank`*, can be rewritten as a power of *$\frac{1}{4}$

$\left(\left(2^{3}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}\right)^{5}$

> *Use the law of indices; *$\left(x^{m}\right)^{n} = x^{m \times n}$

$\left(\left(2^{3}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}\right)^{5} = \left(2^{3 \times \frac{1}{4}}\right)^{5} = \left(2^{\frac{3}{4}}\right)^{5}$

**[1]**

> *Apply the same rule again*

$\left(2^{\frac{3}{4}}\right)^{5} = 2^{\frac{3}{4} \times 5} = 2^{\frac{15}{4}}$

$2^{\frac{15}{4}}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:

$3^{n} = 177147 \times \left(3^{2}\right)^{5}$

**[1]**

> *Use the law of indices; *$\left(x^{n}\right)^{m} = x^{n \times m}$

$3^{n}=177147\times3^{2\times5}\,3^{n}=177147\times3^{10}$

**[1]**

> *Use the fact that we were told; *$177147=3^{11}$

$3^{n}=3^{11}\times3^{10}$

> *Use the law of indices; *$x^{m}\timesx^{n}=x^{m+n}$

$3^{n}=3^{11+10}=3^{21}$

> *Compare both sides of the equation to see the value of *$n$

$n=21$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The mass of a cat is 4.3 kg correct to 2 significant figures.

i) Write down the upper bound of the weight of the cat.

........................... kg [1]

ii) Write down the lower bound of the weight of the cat.

........................... kg [1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) *The next biggest two significant figure that the mass could have rounded to is 4.4. The upper bound for a mass which rounds to 4.3 is halfway between 4.3 and 4.4. The difference between the values is 0.1 so you need to add 0.05 to the rounded value.*

*4.3 + 0.05 = 4.35*

**Upper bound is 4.35 kg** **[1]**

ii) *The next smallest two significant figure that the mass could have rounded to is 4.2. The lower bound for a mass which rounds to 4.3 is halfway between 4.2 and 4.3. The difference between the values is 0.1 so you need to subtract 0.05 from the rounded value.*

*4.3 - 0.05 = 4.25*

**Lower bound is 4.25 kg** **[1]**

**Lower bound is 33.75 cm** **[1]**

i) *The next biggest one decimal place that the length could have rounded to is 33.9. The upper bound for a length which rounds to 33.8 is halfway between 33.8 and 33.9. The difference between the values is 0.1 so you need to add 0.05 to the rounded value.*

*33.8 + 0.05 = 33.85*

[1]

*Lower bound = 18 000 - 500 = 17 500*

**Minimum possible number is 17 500** **[1]**

**Maximum possible number is 18 499** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:

| $d = 54 mm \left(nearest millimetre\right)$ | *53.5    (54 - 0.5)* | *54.5     (54 + 0.5)* |

**One correct bound**** [1]**

*Upper bound: *$\pi = \frac{170 . 5}{53 . 5} = \frac{341}{107} \left(= 3 . 186 915 . . .\right)$* *
*Lower bound: *$\pi = \frac{169 . 5}{54 . 5} = \frac{339}{109} \left(= 3 . 110 091 . . .\right)$

**One correct calculation**** [1]**

**Final answer:** **Upper bound for Dan's value of is 3.187 (4 s.f.) ****[1] **
**Lower bound for Dan's value of is 3.110 (4 s.f.) ****[1]**

**Any value starting with the digits 3.11... are accepted for the lower bound.**

*Upper bound for time is 202.5 minutes    (200 + 2.5)*

$\frac{202.5}{60}=3.375$

**[1]**

*∴ lower bound for average speed is *$\frac{232 . 5}{3 . 375} = 68 . \overset{\cdot}{8}$

**[1]**

**Values in the range 68.8 - 68.9 are accepted.**

parts.solutionMd:
> *This question involves using Pythagoras' theorem.*

$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}$

> *In this case however, we are finding *$c$*, so rearrange*

$c^{2}=a^{2}-b^{2}$

> *As the calculation involves subtraction, the **upper** bound for *$c$* will require *$a$* (and so *$a^{2}$*) to be as **large** as possible - i.e. its **upper** bound and *$b$* to be as **small** as possible - i.e. its **lower** bound.*

$a=8.3\mathrm{cm}=83\mathrm{mm}$* so the upper bound is *$83.5\mathrm{mm}=8.35\mathrm{cm}$*    (83 + 0.5) *
$b=6.1\mathrm{cm}=61\mathrm{mm}$* so the lower bound is *$60.5\mathrm{mm}=6.05\mathrm{cm}$*    (61 - 0.5)*

**Either 8.25, 8.35, 6.05 or 6.15*** ***[1]**

> *Substitute these into the rearranged Pythagoras' theorem.*

$\begin{aligned}c^{2} & = & \left(8 . 35\right)^{2} - \left(6 . 05\right)^{2} \\ c & = & \sqrt{\left(8 . 35\right)^{2} - \left(6 . 05\right)^{2}} = 5 . 754 997 . . .\end{aligned}$

**Using correct bounds**** [1] **
**Using Pythagoras' theorem ****[1]**

**Final answer:** **The upper bound for **$c$** is 5.755 cm (4 s.f.) ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A train travelled along a track in 110 minutes, correct to the nearest 5 minutes.

Could the average speed of the train have been greater than 160 km/h?

parts.solutionMd:
> *The question suggests an **upper** bound - we need to find the largest possible average speed of the train and compare this to 160 km/h. The formula connecting average speed, distance and time is*

$\left(Average\right) Speed = \frac{Distance}{Time}$

> *This is a **division** calculation so for the **upper** bound of average speed we will need **distance** to be as **large** as possible - its **upper** bound, and **time** to be as **small** as possible - its **lower** bound.*

*Upper bound for distance is 275 km    (270 + 5)** *
*Lower bound for time is 107.5 minutes    (110 - 2.5)*

**One from 265, 275, 107.5 or 112.5*** ***[1]**

> *Time given is in minutes so convert this to hours by dividing by 60.*

$\frac{107 . 5}{60} = 1 . 791 \overset{\cdot}{6}$

**[1]**

*∴ upper bound for average speed is *$\frac{275}{1 . 791 \overset{\cdot}{6}} = 153 . 488 372 . . .$

**[1]**

> *Compare this to 160 km/h and answer the question.*

**Final answer:** **The average speed of the train could not have been greater than 160 km/h as the upper bound for its average speed is 153 km/h (3 s.f.) ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Jackson is trying to find the density, in g/cm<sup>3</sup>, of a block of wood. The block of wood is in the shape of a cuboid.

He measures    
the length as 13.2 cm, correct to the nearest mm    
the width as 16.0 cm, correct to the nearest mm    
the height as 21.7 cm, correct to the nearest mm

He measures the mass as 1970 g, correct to the nearest 5 g. 

By considering bounds, work out the density of the wood. 
Give your answer to a suitable degree of accuracy. 

You must show all your working and give a reason for your final answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Both upper and lower bounds (of density) are required. The formulae for density and volume are*

$\begin{aligned}Density & = & \frac{Mass}{Volume} \\ Volume \left(of a cuboid\right) & = & length \times width \times height\end{aligned}$

> *So we need the upper and lower bounds of the length, width, height and mass of the cuboid.*
* With lots of values around, keep them organised using a table*

| *Value* | *Lower bound* | *Upper bound* |
|---|---|---|
| *length* | ***13.15 ****(13.2 - 0.05)* | ***13.25 ****(13.2 + 0.05)* |
| *width* | ***15.95 ****(16.0 - 0.05)* | ***16.05 ****(16.0 + 0.05)* |
| *height* | ***21.65 ****(21.7 - 0.05)* | ***21.75 ****(21.7 + 0.05)* |
| *mass* | ***1967.5 ****(1970 - 2.5)* | ***1972.5 ****(1970 + 2.5)* |

**One correct bound ****[1]**

> *Density is a division calculation so for the **lower** bound of we need the **numerator** to be as **small** as possible - i.e. the **lower** bound of **mass, **and the **denominator** to be as **large** as possible - i.e. the **upper** bound of **volume** (**upper bounds of length**,** width **and** height**).*

*Lower bound of density *$=\frac{1967.5}{13.25\times16.05\times21.75}=0.425367754...$

**Bound for volume**** [1] **
**Bound for density**** [1]**

> *For the **upper** bound of density we need the **numerator** to be as **large** as possible - i.e. the **upper** bound of **mass, **and the **denominator** to be as **small** as possible - i.e. the **lower** bound of **volume** (**lower bounds of length**,** width **and** height**).*

*Upper bound of density *$=\frac{1972.5}{13.15\times15.95\times21.65}=0.434382850...$

> *So we have ...*

$0.425367...<m<0.434382...$

**Both correct ****[1]**

> *To answer the question we need to look for the highest degree of accuracy that both the upper and lower bounds can be rounded to such that they are equal.*

*0.425 367 ... = 0.43 to two significant figures *
*0.434 382 ... = 0.43 to two significant figures*

**To two significant figures the density of the wood is 0.43 g/mm**<sup>**3**</sup>** - this is the highest degree of accuracy to which both the lower and upper bounds agree ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A cycle race across America is 3069.25 miles in length.

Juan knows his average speed for his previous races is 15.12 miles per hour. 
For the next race across America he will cycle for 8 hours per day.

Estimate how many days Juan will take to complete the race.
parts.solutionMd:
> *In this question it is only appropriate to round one of the values to one significant figure. 8 is a single digit number and is already 'nice' to work with.*

*3069.25 miles ≈ 3000 miles*

> *15.12 is roughly half way between 10 and 20 but rounding to either of those would lead to a broad estimate. But to two significant figures it is 15 and this is still quick work with mentally.*

*15.12 miles per hour ≈ 15 miles per hour*

> *Next work out an estimate for the number of miles Juan completes in a day using *$\mathrm{Average} \mathrm{speed}=\frac{\mathrm{Distance}}{\mathrm{Time}}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\therefore Distance \left(per day\right) & = & Average speed per hour \times Hours per day \\ Distance \left(per day\right) & = & 15 \times 8 = 120\end{aligned}$

**Using a correctly rounded value**** [1]**

> *Now estimate the number of days by dividing the total number of miles by the number of miles Juan cycles in a day.*

$\frac{3000}{120}=25$

**[1]**

> *(You can simplify to make the division quicker: *$\frac{3000}{120}=\frac{300}{12}=\frac{50}{2}=25$*).*

**Juan will take approximately 25 days to complete the race ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:

How does this affect your answer to part (a)?
parts.solutionMd:
**Juan's average speed has increased (both from the orginal 15.12 mph and our rounded 15 mph) so he will complete the race more quickly - i.e. in less days**
 **Therefore the answer to part (a) will decrease ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
One uranium atom has a mass of $3.95\times10^{-22}$ grams.

Work out an estimate for the number of uranium atoms in 1 kg of uranium.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by rounding the mass of one uranium atom to one significant figure.*

$3.95\times10^{-22}\approx4\times10^{-22}$

**[1]**

> *Note we have a mixture of grams and kilograms, so convert to grams.*

$1\mathrm{kg}=1000g$

> *The calculation for the number of uranium atoms in 1 kg of uranium will be*

$\mathrm{Number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{atoms}=\frac{\mathrm{Mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{uranium}}{\mathrm{Mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{one} \mathrm{atom}}$

> *Substitute our rounded values in to the formula.*

$\mathrm{Number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{atoms}=\frac{1000}{4\times10^{-22}}$

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1000}{4 \times 10^{- 22}} & = & 0 . 25 \times 10^{25} \\ & & \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *This value is not in standard form (*$A\times10^{n}where1\leqA<10$*).*

*0.25 × 10**<sup>25</sup>** = 2.5 × 10**<sup>-1</sup>** × 10**<sup>25</sup>** = 2.5 × 10**<sup>24</sup>*

**There are approximately 2.5 × 10**<sup>**24**</sup>** atoms in 1 kg of uranium ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Is your answer to (a) an underestimate or an overestimate?

Give a reason for your answer.
parts.solutionMd: **In the calculation **$\frac{1000}{4\times10^{25}}$**, the numerator was left unchanged but the denominator was increased from its actual value** **Therefore the result will be smaller than its real value (dividing by a larger number) so our estimate is an underestimate ****[1]**
