parts.problemMd:
$a=\sqrt{8}+2$ 
$b=\sqrt{8}-2$ 
$T=a^{2}-b^{2}$

Show that $T=c\sqrt{2}$ stating the value of $c$
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1* 
*Find **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by multiplying √8 + 2 by itself)*

$\begin{aligned}a^{2} & = & \left(\sqrt{8} + 2\right) \left(\sqrt{8} + 2\right) \\ & = & \sqrt{8} \times \sqrt{8} + \sqrt{8} \times 2 + 2 \times \sqrt{8} + 2 \times 2\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Simplify the terms (using the surd law *$\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{a} = \left(\sqrt{a}\right)^{2} = a$* for the first term)* * *

$\begin{aligned}a^{2} & = & 8 + 2 \sqrt{8} + 2 \sqrt{8} + 4 \\ & = & 12 + 4 \sqrt{8}\end{aligned}$ * *

> *Find **b*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by multiplying √8 - 2 by itself) and do the same steps as above  *

$\begin{aligned}b^{2} & = & \left(\sqrt{8} - 2\right) \left(\sqrt{8} - 2\right) \\ & = & \sqrt{8} \times \sqrt{8} - \sqrt{8} \times 2 - 2 \times \sqrt{8} + 2 \times 2 \\ & = & 8 - 2 \sqrt{8} - 2 \sqrt{8} + 4 \\ & = & 12 - 4 \sqrt{8}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2*</sup>* by subtracting the two results above (using brackets around the results) Collect like terms  *

$\begin{aligned}a^{2} - b^{2} & = & \left(12 + 4 \sqrt{8}\right) - \left(12 - 4 \sqrt{8}\right) \\ & = & 12 + 4 \sqrt{8} - 12 + 4 \sqrt{8} \\ & = & 8 \sqrt{8}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The result must be given in the form **c**√2 where** c** is an integer (whole number) *
*Write *$\sqrt{8}$* as *$2\sqrt{2}$* (from *$\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{4\times2}=\sqrt{4}\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}$*)  *

$\begin{aligned}a^{2} - b^{2} & = & 8 \times 2 \sqrt{2} \\ & = & 16 \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$

$16\sqrt{2}$** (where ****c**** = 16)*** ***[1]**

*Method 2*** **
*Use the "difference of two squares" to factorise **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2*</sup>*  *

$a^{2} - b^{2} = \left(a + b\right) \left(a - b\right)$

**[1]**

> *Substitute **a** = √8 + 2 and **b** = √8 - 2 into the expression and collect like terms  *

$\begin{aligned}a^{2} - b^{2} & = & \left(\sqrt{8} + 2 + \sqrt{8} - 2\right) \left(\sqrt{8} + 2 - \left(\sqrt{8} - 2\right)\right) \\ & = & \left(2 \sqrt{8}\right) \left(\sqrt{8} + 2 - \sqrt{8} + 2\right) \\ & = & \left(2 \sqrt{8}\right) \left(4\right) \\ & = & 8 \sqrt{8}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The result must be given in the form **c**√2 where** c** is an integer (whole number) Write *$\sqrt{8}$* as *$2\sqrt{2}$* (from *$\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{4\times2}=\sqrt{4}\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}$*)  *

$\begin{aligned}a^{2} - b^{2} & = & 8 \times 2 \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify the final answer (using 8 × 2 = 16)*

$16\sqrt{2}$** (where ****c**** = 16)*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Show that $\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right)^{2} - \left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right)^{2} = 8 \sqrt{3}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1* 
*Find (2 + √3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by multiplying 2 + √3 by itself)*

$\begin{aligned}\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right) \left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right) & = & 2 \times 2 + 2 \times \sqrt{3} + \sqrt{3} \times 2 + \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$

*Simplify the terms (using the surd law *$\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{a} = \left(\sqrt{a}\right)^{2} = a$* for the last term) then collect like terms* * *

$\begin{aligned} & = & 4 + 2 \sqrt{3} + 2 \sqrt{3} + 3 \\ & = & 7 + 4 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find (2 - √3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by multiplying 2 - √3 by itself) and do the same steps as above  *

$\begin{aligned}\left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right) \left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right) & = & 2 \times 2 - 2 \times \sqrt{3} - \sqrt{3} \times 2 + \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} \\ & = & 4 - 2 \sqrt{3} - 2 \sqrt{3} + 3 \\ & = & 7 - 4 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Find (2 + √3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* - (2 - √3)*<sup>*2*</sup>*  by subtracting the two results above (using brackets around the results) *
*Collect like terms  *

$\begin{aligned}\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right)^{2} - \left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right)^{2} & = & \left(7 + 4 \sqrt{3}\right) - \left(7 - 4 \sqrt{3}\right) \\ & = & 7 + 4 \sqrt{3} - 7 + 4 \sqrt{3} \\ & = & 8 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$

$8\sqrt{3}$** *** ***[1]**

*Method 2*** **
*Use the "difference of two squares" to factorise **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2*</sup>*  *

$a^{2} - b^{2} = \left(a + b\right) \left(a - b\right)$

**[1]**

> *Substitute **a** = 2 + √3 and **b** = 2 - √3 into the expression and collect like terms  *

$\begin{aligned}a^{2} - b^{2} & = & \left(2 + \sqrt{3} + 2 - \sqrt{3}\right) \left(2 + \sqrt{3} - \left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right)\right) \\ & = & \left(4\right) \left(2 + \sqrt{3} - 2 + \sqrt{3}\right) \\ & = & 4 \left(2 \sqrt{3}\right) \\ & = & 8 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$

$8\sqrt{3}$* ***[1]**

**[1]**

> *Multiply the numerators together and multiply the denominators together*

*Use that √3 × √3 = 3* * *

$\frac{12\sqrt{3}}{3}$ * *

*Cancel the whole-number parts of the fraction (by dividing top-and-bottom by 3)* * *

$\frac{{}^{4}{\cancel{12}} \sqrt{3}}{{}^{1}{\cancel{3}}}$

$4\sqrt{3}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Show that $\left(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{8}\right)^{2} = 18$
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1* 
*Write √8 in terms of √2 (using the surd law *$\sqrt{ab}=\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{b}$*)* * *

$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{8} & = & \sqrt{4 \times 2} \\ & = & \sqrt{4} \times \sqrt{2} \\ & = & 2 \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$ * *

*Collect the √2 and 2√2 inside the brackets* * *

$\left(\sqrt{2} + 2 \sqrt{2}\right)^{2} = \left(3 \sqrt{2}\right)^{2}$

**[1]**

*Square 3√2, using the index law *$\left(a b\right)^{n} = a^{n} b^{n}$* and that (√2)*<sup>*2*</sup>* = 2* * *

$3^{2} \left(\sqrt{2}\right)^{2} = 9 \times 2$

**18*** ***[1]**

*Method 2* 
*Write as the product of two brackets* * *

$\left(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{8}\right) \left(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{8}\right)$ * *

*Expand the brackets (by multiplying all terms in the first bracket by all terms in the second bracket)* * *

$\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{8}+\sqrt{8}\times\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{8}\times\sqrt{8}$

**[1]**

*Simplify the first and last terms (using the surd law *$\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{a} = \left(\sqrt{a}\right)^{2} = a$*)* * *

$2+\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{8}+\sqrt{8}\times\sqrt{2}+8$ * *

*Simplify the middle two terms (using the surd law *$\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{b}=\sqrt{a\timesb}$*)* * *

$2+\sqrt{2\times8}+\sqrt{8\times2}+8\,=2+\sqrt{16}+\sqrt{16}+8$ * *

*Write √16 as 4 (from 4 × 4 = 16)* * *

$2+4+4+8$

**18*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Show that  $\frac{6-\sqrt{8}}{\sqrt{2}-1}$  can be written in the form $a+b\sqrt{2}$  where $a$ and $b$ are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
*Rationalise the denominator (by multiplying top-and-bottom by √2 + 1)* *(-√2 - 1 would also work)* *   *

$\frac{6-\sqrt{8}}{\sqrt{2}-1}\times\frac{\sqrt{2}+1}{\sqrt{2}+1}$

**[1]**

*Multiply the numerators together and multiply the denominators together* * *

$\frac{\left(6 - \sqrt{8}\right) \left(\sqrt{2} + 1\right)}{\left(\sqrt{2} - 1\right) \left(\sqrt{2} + 1\right)}$ * *

*Expand the brackets*

$\frac{6\times\sqrt{2}+6\times1-\sqrt{8}\times\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{8}\times1}{\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2}\times1-1\times\sqrt{2}-1\times1}$

**[1]**

*Simplify the terms (using the surd laws *$\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{a} = \left(\sqrt{a}\right)^{2} = a$* and *$\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{b}=\sqrt{a\timesb}$*)* * *

> $\frac{6\sqrt{2}+6-\sqrt{16}-\sqrt{8}}{2-1}\,=\frac{6\sqrt{2}+6-4-\sqrt{8}}{1}\,=6\sqrt{2}+2-\sqrt{8}$*  *

> *The final answer must be in the form **a **+ **b**√2 where **a** and **b** are integers (whole numbers) Write *$\sqrt{8}$* as *$2\sqrt{2}$* (from *$\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{4\times2}=\sqrt{4}\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}$*) and collect like terms  *

> $=6\sqrt{2}+2-2\sqrt{2}\,=4\sqrt{2}+2$*  *

> *This can be rewritten as 2 + 4√2, which is the correct form of the answer*

$2+4\sqrt{2}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Show that $\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right) \left(3 - \sqrt{2}\right) = 1 + 2 \sqrt{2}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Expand the brackets (by multiplying each term in the first bracket by each term in the second bracket)* * *

$1 \\times 3 + 1 \\times ( - \sqrt{2} ) + \sqrt{2} \\times 3 + \sqrt{2} \\times ( - \sqrt{2} )$
$= 3 - \sqrt{2} + 3 \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} \\times \sqrt{2}$

**[1]**

*Simplify the last term (using the surd law *$\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{a} = \left(\sqrt{a}\right)^{2} = a$*) and collect any like terms* * *

$=3+2\sqrt{2}-2\,=1+2\sqrt{2}$ * *

> *This is now in the form** a** + **b**√2 where **a** and **b** are integers (whole numbers, **a** = 1 and **b** = 2)*

$1+2\sqrt{2}$** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd: Show that $\left(\sqrt{12} - \sqrt{3}\right)^{2} = 3$
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1* 
*Write √12 in terms of √3 (using the surd law *$\sqrt{ab}=\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{b}$*)* * *

$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{12} & = & \sqrt{4 \times 3} \\ & = & \sqrt{4} \times \sqrt{3} \\ & = & 2 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$ * *

*Collect the 2√3 and √3 inside the brackets* * *

$\left(2 \sqrt{3} - \sqrt{3}\right)^{2} = \left(\sqrt{3}\right)^{2}$

**[1]**

*Square √3* * *

$\left(\sqrt{3}\right)^{2} = 3$

**3*** ***[1]**

*Method 2* 
*Write as the product of two brackets* * *

$\left(\sqrt{12} - \sqrt{3}\right) \left(\sqrt{12} - \sqrt{3}\right)$ * *

*Expand the brackets (by multiplying all terms in the first bracket by all terms in the second bracket)* * *

$\sqrt{12}\times\sqrt{12}-\sqrt{12}\times\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{12}+\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}$

**[1]**

*Simplify the first and last terms (using the surd law *$\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{a} = \left(\sqrt{a}\right)^{2} = a$*)* * *

$12-\sqrt{12}\times\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{12}\times\sqrt{3}+3$ * *

*Simplify the middle two terms (using the surd law *$\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{b}=\sqrt{a\timesb}$*)* * *

$12-\sqrt{12\times3}-\sqrt{12\times3}+3\,=12-\sqrt{36}-\sqrt{36}+3$ * *

*Write √36 as 6 (from 6 × 6 = 36)* * *

$12-6-6+3$

**3*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Show that $\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}$ can be written as $2-\sqrt{2}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1* 
*Multiply top-and-bottom by √2* * *

$\frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{ \sqrt{2} }} \\times \frac{ \sqrt{2} }{ \sqrt{2} }$
$= \frac{ \sqrt{2} }{ \sqrt{2} ( 1 + \frac{1}{ \sqrt{2} } )}$
$= \frac{ \sqrt{2} }{ \sqrt{2} + 1}$

**[1]**

*Rationalise the denominator (by multiplying top-and-bottom by √2 - 1)* *(-√2 + 1 would also work)* *   *

$\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}+1}\times\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{\sqrt{2}-1}$

**[1]**

*Multiply the numerators together and multiply the denominators together* * *

$\frac{\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{2}\times1}{\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2}\times1-1\times\sqrt{2}-1\times1}$ * *

*Simplify the terms (using the surd law *$\sqrt{a} \times \sqrt{a} = \left(\sqrt{a}\right)^{2} = a$*)* * *

> $\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{2-1}\,=\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{1}$*  *

> *The final answer is 2 - √2*

$2-\sqrt{2}$* ***[1]**

*Method 2* 
*Rationalise the denominator of *$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$* (by multiplying top-and-bottom by √2)* *Use that √2 × √2 = 2* * *

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\times\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}\,=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ * *

*Write out the fraction using this result* * *

$\frac{1}{1+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}$

**[1]**

*Rationalise the denominator (by multiplying top-and-bottom by *$1-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$*)* *(Another way is to first multiply top-and-bottom by 2, then rationalise the denominator)* * *

$\frac{1}{\left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)} \times \frac{\left(1 - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}{\left(1 - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}$

**[1]**

*Expand the denominator (for example, using the difference of two squares, (**a** + **b**)(**a** - **b**) = **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2*</sup>*)* * *

$\frac{1-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{1-\frac{2}{4}}\,=\frac{1-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{\frac{1}{2}}$ * *

*Dividing by a half is the same as multiplying by 2 (*$\div\frac{1}{2}$* means *$\times\frac{2}{1}$*)* * *

$= 2 ( 1 - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} )$
$= 2 - \sqrt{2}$

$2-\sqrt{2}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd:
$\begin{aligned}a & = & \sqrt{8} + 4 \\ b & = & \sqrt{8} - 4\end{aligned}$

$(a--b)(a+b)$ can be written in the form $y\sqrt{4y}$

Find the value of $y$ 
Show your working clearly.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Substitute the values of **a** and **b** into the expression*

$\left(a - b\right) \left(a + b\right) = \left(\left(\sqrt{8} + 4\right) - \left(\sqrt{8} - 4\right)\right) \times \left(\left(\sqrt{8} + 4\right) + \left(\sqrt{8} - 4\right)\right)$

> *Simplify the expressions*

$\left(\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{8} + 4 - - 4\right) \times \left(\sqrt{8} + \sqrt{8} + 4 - 4\right) = \left(8\right) \times \left(2 \sqrt{8}\right) = 16 \sqrt{8}$

**Any equivalent to **$16\sqrt{8}$** e.g. **$32\sqrt{2}$** ****[2]**

*We need to rewrite in the form *$y\sqrt{4y}$ *Note that this is not as easy as finding the simplest form of the surd*

> *Consider writing *$y\sqrt{4y}$* in a different way, which may be easier*

$y\sqrt{4y}=y\times\sqrt{4}\times\sqrt{y}=2y\sqrt{y}$

*This is more similar to our answer of *$16\sqrt{8}$*, and in this case *$y=8$ *As the two forms are equivalent, and *$y=8$*, we could write the answer using *$y\sqrt{4y}$

$8\sqrt{4\times8}$ **[1]**

> $\frac{31}{\sqrt{31}}$*  *

> * *

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd: Show that $\sqrt{5} \left(\sqrt{8} + \sqrt{18}\right)$ can be written in the form $a\sqrt{10}$ and state the value of $a$. You must show your full working.

**[1]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd: Show that $\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{12}$ can be rewritten as $3\sqrt{3}$

parts.problemMd: Show that $\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^{7} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{81}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Rationalise the denominator of *$\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$* (by multiplying top-and-bottom by √3)* * *

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}$

**[1]*** *

*Multiply the numerators together and multiply the denominators together* *Use √3 × √3 = 3* * *

$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ * *

*Put this result back into the question* * *

$\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)^{7}$ * *

*Apply the power outside the fraction to both the numerator and the denominator (using the index law *$\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{n} = \frac{a^{n}}{b^{n}}$*)* * *

$\frac{\left(\sqrt{3}\right)^{7}}{3^{7}}$ * *

*You do not need to work out 3*<sup>*7*</sup>* (this is hard without a calculator)* *Simplify (√3)*<sup>*7*</sup>* (by writing it out as a multiplication and using √3 × √3 = 3)* * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(\sqrt{3}\right)^{7} & = & \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} \\ & = & \left(\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3}\right) \times \left(\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3}\right) \times \left(\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3}\right) \times \sqrt{3} \\ & = & 3 \times 3 \times 3 \times \sqrt{3} \\ & = & 3^{3} \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]*** *

*Put this numerator back into the question and cancel the powers of 3 (by dividing top-and-bottom by 3*<sup>*3*</sup>*)* * *

$\frac{3^{3}\sqrt{3}}{3^{7}}\,=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3^{4}}$ * *

> *Work out 3*<sup>*4*</sup>* (by doing 3 × 3 × 3 × 3)*

$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{81}$* ***[1]**

$\frac{\sqrt{2187}}{2187}$** is also accepted **

parts.problemMd:
The area of a rectangle is $18$ $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$

The length of the rectangle is $\left(\sqrt{7 } + 1\right)$ $\mathrm{cm}$.

Without using a calculator and showing each stage of your working, find the width of the rectangle.

Give your answer in the form $a\sqrt{b}+c$ where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers.

.....................$\mathrm{cm}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The area of a rectangle is found by multiplying the two perpendicular lengths together. One of the lengths can be found by dividing the area by the other length.*

$\mathrm{Length}=\frac{18}{\sqrt{7}+1}$

> *You need to rationalise the denominator. Multiply the top and bottom of the fraction by the denominator with the sign in the middle changed.*

$\frac{18}{\left(\sqrt{7} + 1\right)} \times \frac{\left(\sqrt{7} - 1\right)}{\left(\sqrt{7} - 1\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Expand the brackets. Simplify the bottom.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{18 \sqrt{7} - 18}{7 - \sqrt{7} + \sqrt{7} - 1} & = & \frac{18 \sqrt{7} - 18}{6}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Cancel out the common factor of 6.*

$(3\sqrt{7}-3)\mathrm{cm}$* ***[1]**

parts.solutionMd:

$\frac{4}{7 - \sqrt{5}} \times \frac{7 + \sqrt{5}}{7 + \sqrt{5}} = \frac{4 \left(7 + \sqrt{5}\right)}{\left(7 - \sqrt{5}\right) \left(7 + \sqrt{5}\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Expand the top and bottom of the fraction, and simplify the terms*

$\frac{4 \left(7 + \sqrt{5}\right)}{\left(7 - \sqrt{5}\right) \left(7 + \sqrt{5}\right)} = \frac{28 + 4 \sqrt{5}}{7^{2} - 7 \sqrt{5} + 7 \sqrt{5} - \left(\sqrt{5}\right)^{2}} = \frac{28 + 4 \sqrt{5}}{49 - 5} = \frac{28 + 4 \sqrt{5}}{44}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify the fraction by dividing the top and bottom by 4*

$\frac{28+4\sqrt{5}}{44}=\frac{7+\sqrt{5}}{11}$

> *Rewrite in required format*

$\frac{7}{11}+\frac{1}{11}\sqrt{5}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a cuboid with a square cross section.

![3D rectangular prism diagram with dimensions x cm by x cm by (2√5 - 3) cm. Text indicates the diagram is not drawn to scale.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/number/surds/assets/001-3d-rectangular-prism-diagram-with-dimensions-x-c.png)

The volume of the cuboid is $\left(13 + 6 \sqrt{5}\right)$cm<sup>3</sup>

Without using a calculator, find the value of $x$
Give your answer in the form $a+\sqrt{b}$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers. 
Show your working clearly
parts.solutionMd:
> *Form an equation for the volume*

$x^{2} \left(2 \sqrt{5} - 3\right) = \left(13 + 6 \sqrt{5}\right)$

> *Divide to get *$x^{2}$

$x^{2}=\frac{13+6\sqrt{5}}{2\sqrt{5}-3}$

> *[M1]*

> *Rationalise the denominator*

$\frac{13+6\sqrt{5}}{2\sqrt{5}-3}\times\frac{2\sqrt{5}+3}{2\sqrt{5}+3}$

**[M1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You could also rationalise the denominator by working out $\frac{13+6\sqrt{5}}{2\sqrt{5}-3}\times\frac{-2\sqrt{5}-3}{-2\sqrt{5}-3}$. It will lead to the same answer.

> *Multiply the fractions and simplify*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} & = & \frac{\left(13 + 6 \sqrt{5}\right) \left(2 \sqrt{5} + 3\right)}{\left(2 \sqrt{5} - 3\right) \left(2 \sqrt{5} + 3\right)} \\ x^{2} & = & \frac{26 \sqrt{5} + 39 + 60 + 18 \sqrt{5}}{20 - 9} \\ x^{2} & = & \frac{44 \sqrt{5} + 99}{11} \\ x^{2} & = & 4 \sqrt{5} + 9\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *You want *$x$* in the form *$a+\sqrt{b}$*, so square this and equate it to your previous answer*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & a + \sqrt{b} \\ x^{2} & = & \left(a + \sqrt{b}\right)^{2} \\ x^{2} & = & a^{2} + 2 a \sqrt{b} + b\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}4 \sqrt{5} + 9 & = & a^{2} + 2 a \sqrt{b} + b\end{aligned}$

> *Compare the terms of the equation*

$2a\sqrt{b}=4\sqrt{5}\mathrm{and}a^{2}+b=9$

$b=5\mathrm{and}2a=4$*  so *$a=2$

$x=2+\sqrt{5}$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd: Show that  $\left(5 \sqrt{3} - \sqrt{12}\right)^{2}$  simplifies to an integer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Write the expression out in full*

*Expand the brackets* 
*Be careful with the last term, where a negative multiplied by a negative makes a positive *

$( 5 \sqrt{3} \\times 5 \sqrt{3} ) - ( 5 \sqrt{3} \\times \sqrt{12} ) - ( 5 \sqrt{3} \\times \sqrt{12} ) + ( \sqrt{12} \\times \sqrt{12} )$
$= ( 5 \sqrt{3} \\times 5 \sqrt{3} ) - 2 ( 5 \sqrt{3} \\times \sqrt{12} ) + ( \sqrt{12} \\times \sqrt{12} )$

**Accurate expansion ****[1]**

> *Simplify some of the surds using *$\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{a}=a$* and combine the integers*

$\begin{aligned} & & \left(5 \times 5 \times 3\right) - 2 \left(5 \sqrt{3} \sqrt{12}\right) + \left(12\right) \\ & = & \left(75\right) - 2 \left(5 \sqrt{3} \sqrt{12}\right) + 12 \\ & = & 87 - 2 \left(5 \sqrt{3} \sqrt{12}\right)\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & & 87 - 2 \left(5 \times \sqrt{3 \times 12}\right) \\ & = & 87 - 2 \left(5 \times \sqrt{36}\right) \\ & = & 87 - 2 \left(5 \times 6\right) \\ & = & 87 - 2 \left(30\right) \\ & = & 27\end{aligned}$

**Reducing to 3 integers ****[1]**

**27 ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Rationalise the denominator of  $\frac{4}{7-\sqrt{5}}$

Show each stage of your working.

Give your answer in the form $a+b\sqrt{5}$ where $a$ and $b$ are fractions in their simplest forms.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[exam-tip]**
> Rationalising the denominator is the process of eliminating radicals (like square roots/surds) from the denominator of a fraction.
> 
> The process involves multiplying the fraction by the value of 1 using suitable expressions.

> *Use the inverse operation of the denominator to select an expression to multiply the numerator and denominator by*

*The inverse operation of *$7-\sqrt{5}$* is *$7+\sqrt{5}$

> *Multiplying the fraction by *$\frac{7+\sqrt{5}}{7+\sqrt{5}}$*will eliminate the surd from the denominator*

$\frac{4}{\left(7 - \sqrt{5}\right)} \times \frac{\left(7 + \sqrt{5}\right)}{\left(7 + \sqrt{5}\right)}$

**[M1]**

> *Multiply the fractions, expand the double brackets on the denominator and apply the laws of surds*

$\frac{4 \left(7 + \sqrt{5}\right)}{\left(7 - \sqrt{5}\right) \left(7 + \sqrt{5}\right)} = \frac{28 + 4 \sqrt{5}}{49 - 7 \sqrt{5} + 7 \sqrt{5} - \sqrt{25}}$

**[M1]**

> *Simplify terms*

$\frac{28+4\sqrt{5}}{49-5}=\frac{28+4\sqrt{5}}{44}$

> *Divide each term by the highest common factor (HCF) to simplify the fraction, in this case the HCF is 4*

$\frac{7+\sqrt{5}}{11}$

> *Leave in the form *$a+b\sqrt{5}$* by separating the terms in the numerator each with a denominator of 11*

$\frac{7}{11}+\frac{1}{11}\sqrt{5}$

**[A1]**

$π\times8.5^{2}=72.25π$

**[M1]**

parts.problemMd:
![q1-4-5-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/019-q1-4-5-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

$ABCD$ is a square with a side length of $4x$

 $N$ is the point on $AD$ where $ND=x$

Find an expression, in terms of $x$, for the area of triangle $BMN$. Give your expression in its simplest form.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1:*

> *Calculate the area of the square **ABCD**.*

$4x\times4x=16x^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Calculate the area of the triangle **ABN, **using *$A=\frac{1}{2}bh$*, where *$b$* is the base of the triangle and *$h$* is its perpendicular height.*

![4-5-12](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/020-4-5-12.png)

$A=\frac{1}{2}\times4x\times3x$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$A=6x^{2}$

> *Calculate the area of the triangle **BMC**.*

![4-5-11](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/021-4-5-11.png)

$A=\frac{1}{2}\times4x\times2x$

> *Simplify.*

$A=4x^{2}$

> *Calculate the area of the triangle **MND**.*

![4-5-13](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/022-4-5-13.png)

$A=\frac{1}{2}\timesx\times2x$

> *Simplify.*

$A=x^{2}$

> *Find the area of the shaded triangle **BNM** by subtracting the area of triangles **BMC **and** ABN **from the area of the square** ABCD.*

$16x^{2}-6x^{2}-4x^{2}-x^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$5x^{2}$* ***[1]**

** **

> *Method 2:*

> *Calculate the length **NM** on the right-angled triangle **NDM**, using Pythagoras' theorem, *$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$*.*

> *Substitute the given values into the formula.*

> $x^{2} + \left(2 x\right)^{2} = N M^{2}$* *

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} + 4 x^{2} & = & N M^{2} \\ 5 x^{2} & = & N M^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Take the square root of both sides.*

$\sqrt{5}x=NM$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}4 x^{2} + 16 x^{2} & = & B M^{2} \\ 20 x^{2} & = & B M^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Take the square root of both sides.*

$\sqrt{20}x=BM$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$2\sqrt{5}x=BM$

parts.problemMd:
![q20-4ma1-2h-qp-jan21-paper2-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/034-q20-4ma1-2h-qp-jan21-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

The diagram shows a shaded region $T$ formed by removing an equilateral triangle$PQR$from a regular hexagon $ABCDEF$.

The points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ such that $AB=1.5\timesPQ$.

Given that the area of region $T$ is $72\sqrt{3}\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ work out the length of $PQ$.

......................................................$\mathrm{cm}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for a triangle is *$A=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$* where **a **and **b **are the lengths of two sides that form angle **C**.** *
*Let **x** denote the length **PQ**. Triangle **PQR** is an equilateral triangle so all the lengths are equal and all the angles are 60°. Find the area by substituting **a** = **x**, **b** = **x **and **C** = 60. Simplify the expression,*

$\begin{aligned}Area of P Q R & = & \frac{1}{2} \times x \times x \times sin \left(60\right) \\ & = & \frac{1}{2} \times x \times x \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ & = & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} x^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The length **PQ** = 1.5**x**. A regular hexagon is made up of 6 equilateral triangles. *
*Find the area of the hexagon by finding substituting **a** = 1.5**x**, **b** = 1.5**x** and **C** = 60 into the formula and multiplying by 6.*

$\begin{aligned}Area of A B C D E F & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 1 . 5 x \times 1 . 5 x \times sin \left(60\right) \times 6 \\ & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 1 . 5 x \times 1 . 5 x \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times 6 \\ & = & \frac{27 \sqrt{3}}{8} x^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Form an equation using the fact that the difference between the area of the triangle and the hexagon is equal to *$72\sqrt{3}$* cm*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{27 \sqrt{3}}{8} x^{2} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} x^{2} & = & 72 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides √3 and multiply both sides by 8. Then solve the equation to find **x **(which is a positive value so you can ignore the negative square root).*

$\begin{aligned}27 x^{2} - 2 x^{2} & = & 576 \\ 25 x^{2} & = & 576 \\ x^{2} & = & \frac{576}{25} \\ x & = & \sqrt{\frac{576}{25}} \\ x & = & \frac{24}{5}\end{aligned}$

**The length of ****PQ**** is 4.8 cm ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Calvin has $12$ identical rectangular tiles. He arranges the tiles to fit exactly round the edge of a shaded rectangle, as shown in the diagram below.

![q5-paper2h-jan2019-edexcel-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/013-q5-paper2h-jan2019-edexcel-igcse-maths.png)

Work out the area of the shaded rectangle.
parts.solutionMd:
*Call the longer length of the tile **x** and the smaller length **y**.* 
*4 long lengths and one short length make up the length of 123 cm.* 
*2 long lengths and one short length make up the length of 67 cm.* 
*Form two equations with this information.*

$\begin{aligned}4 x + y & = & 123 \\ 2 x + y & = & 67\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract the equations to eliminate the **y** variable. Then solve for **x**.*

$4 x + \cancel{y} = 123 - \left(2 x + \cancel{y} = 67\right) 2 x = 56 x = 28$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the value of **x** back into one of the equations to find **y**.*

$\begin{aligned}4 \left(28\right) + y & = & 123 \\ 112 + y & = & 123 \\ y & = & 11\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The area of the shaded bit can be found by finding the area of the whole rectangle and subtracting the area of 12 tiles.*

$123\times67-12\times28\times11=4545$

**[1]**

> *Include the units for the area.*

**Area is**** 4545 cm**<sup>**2**</sup> **[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the area of the trapezium using: *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the lengths of the parallel edges and *$h$* is the perpendicular height.*

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a regular octagon $ABCDEFGH.$

![q22-paper1hr-nov2020-edexcel-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/026-q22-paper1hr-nov2020-edexcel-igcse-maths.png)

Find the area of the shaded region $ACDEH.$ 
Give your answer correct to the nearest $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$

............................................. $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the interior angle of the regular octagon using: *$size of interior angle = \frac{180 \left(n - 2\right)}{n}$*, where *$n$* is the number of sides of the polygon.*

$\frac{180 \left(8 - 2\right)}{8} = 135 \circ$

**[1]**

> *Therefore angle **ABC** = 135°, and triangle **ABC **is an isosceles triangle with sides of 10cm. Mark this on the diagram.*

![ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/027-ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7.png)

> *Triangle **ABC **is an isosceles triangle, so angle **BAC **= angle **BCA **= 1/2(180 - 135). *

*Angle ***BAC ***= Angle ***BCA ***= ** *$\frac{180-135}{2}=22.5^{\circ}$

> *Find angles **ACD **and **CAD **in triangle **ACD.*

![ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7-diagram-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/028-ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7-diagram-2.png)

*Angle ***ACD*** = Angle ***BCD*** - Angle ***ABC*** = 135 - 22.5 = 112.5°*

*Angle ***CAD*** = Angle ***BAH ***- Angle ***DAH*** - Angle ***BAC ***= 135 - 90 - 22.5 = 22.5°*

> *To find the length of **AD, y**ou know the length of one side (**CD**) and the angle opposite it (**CAD**). You also know angle **ACD** so you can find the length of the side opposite that using the sine rule.*

> *The formula for the sine rule is *$\frac{a}{\mathrm{sin}A}=\frac{b}{\mathrm{sin}B}$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that are opposite the angles **A **and **B **respectively. Substitute **a** = **AD**, **b** = 10, **A** = 112.5 and **B** = 22.5 into the formula.*

$\frac{A D}{sin \left(112 . 5\right)} = \frac{10}{sin \left(22 . 5\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by sin(112.5) and type into your calculator.*

$\begin{aligned}A D & = & \frac{10}{sin \left(22 . 5\right)} \times sin \left(112 . 5\right) \\ & = & 24 . 14213 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Now find the area of rectangle **ADEH.*

**Area ADEH ***= 24.14213... × 10 = 241.4213... cm**<sup>2</sup>*

**[1]**

> *Now look at triangle **ACD**.*

![ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7-diagram-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/029-ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7-diagram-3.png)

> *Find angle **ADC.*

*Angle ***ADC*** = Angle ***CDE*** - Angle ***ADE*** = 135 - 90 = 45°*

> *The formula for the area of a triangle is *$\mathrm{Area}=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that form angle **C**. Substitute **a** = 24.14213..., **b** = 10 and **C** = 45 into the formula.*

$\begin{aligned}Area & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 24 . 14213 . . . \times 10 \times sin \left(45\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Type into your calculator.*

$\begin{aligned}Area_{A C D} & = & 85 . 35531 . . . cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the shaded area by adding the area of the rectangle to the area of the triangle.*

$\begin{aligned}Area & = & 241 . 4213 . . . + 85 . 35531 . . . = 326 . 776 . . . cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Round to 3 significant figures. Remember to include the units for the area.*

$\mathrm{Area}=327\mathrm{cm}^{2}(3\mathrm{sf})$ **[1]**
** Answers from 326 - 327 accepted.**

![q25-4ma1-1h-qp-june21-paper1-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/010-q25-4ma1-1h-qp-june21-paper1-igcse-maths.png)

One of the circles has centre $O$ and radius 5cm.

Calculate the area of region $R$.

parts.solutionMd:
> *The area of the region **R **is the area of the larger segment from circle centre **O** added to the area of the smaller segment from circle centre **P**. *

![ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q4-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/011-ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q4-diagram-1.png)

> *To find the area of the segment in circle centre **O, **subtract the area of triangle **AOB **from the area of sector **AOB.*

> *Find the area of triangle **AOB** using the area of a triangle formula, *$A=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the two known sides and *$C$* is the included angle. **OA **and **OB **are both radii so are both equal to 5 cm.*

$A r e a_{t r i a n g l e A O B} = \frac{1}{2} \times \left(5\right) \times \left(5\right) \times sin \left(50\right) = \frac{25}{2} sin 50$

> *It is best to leave working as exact values as you work through the problem, but if you choose to round make sure you use at least 4 significant figures throughout. *

> *To find the area of the sector, you will first need to find its radius. You know the lengths of two sides and the angle between them of the triangle and the radius of the sector is the side opposite the angle, so you can use the cosine rule, *$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\mathrm{cos}A$*, where **b** and **c** are the lengths of the two sides that form angle **A** and **a** is the length of the side opposite **A**.*

$r ^{2} = 26 ^{2} + 15 ^{2} - 2 ( 26 ) ( 15 ) cos ( 38 )$

**Correct fraction**** [1] **
**Correct method to find area**** [1]**

parts.solutionMd:

The perimeter of the trapezium is 56 cm.

parts.solutionMd:
> *Split 56 cm in the ratio 5 : 12 : 6 : 5 to find the length of each side of the trapezium.*

> *Add the parts of the ratio together.*

$5+12+6+5=28$

> *Divide 56 by the total number of ratio parts.*

$56\div28=2$

**[1]**

> *Multiply each part of the ratio by 2 to find the lengths of each side.*

$\mathrm{AD}=5\times2=10\mathrm{cm}\,\mathrm{AB}=12\times2=24\mathrm{cm}\,\mathrm{DC}=6\times2=12\mathrm{cm}\,\mathrm{BC}=5\times2=10\mathrm{cm}$

**[1]**

> *The area of a trapezium can be found using the formula *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the parallel sides and *$h$* is the **perpendicular **height.  *
*The perpendicular height is not known, but can be found using Pythagoras' theorem. The trapezium is an isosceles trapezium so the property that there is a line of symmetry down the middle can be used.*

![_Fylc3vx_ocr-gcse-tq-ma-are-and-perimeter-vh-q4-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/033-fylc3vx-ocr-gcse-tq-ma-are-and-perimeter-vh-q4-d.png)

> *Find the distance from the point **X **(the base of the perpendicular height) to the point B.*

$XB=\frac{24-12}{2}=6\mathrm{cm}$

**[1]**

> *Use Pythagoras' theorem *$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$* with the sides XB, CX and BC to find the perpendicular height of the trapezium.*

$\begin{aligned}h^{2 } + X B^{2} & = & BC^{2} \\ h^{2 } + 6^{2} & = & 10^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange and solve to find **h.*

$\begin{aligned}h^{2 } & = & 10^{2} - 6^{2} \\ & = & 100 - 36 \\ & = & 64 \\ h & = & \sqrt{64} \\ & = & 8 cm\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute into the formula for the area of a trapezium,  *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a=\mathrm{AB}=24\mathrm{cm}$*, *$b=\mathrm{CD}=12\mathrm{cm}$*and *$h=8\mathrm{cm}$*.*

$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(24 + 12\right) \times 8$

**[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The perimeter of a right-angled triangle is 72 cm.
 The lengths of its sides are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5.

Work out the area of the triangle.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First add up the ratio numbers to find how many 'parts' the ratio divides the perimeter into. *
*Then divide the perimeter by that sum to find the size of one part.*

$3+4+5=12\,\,72\div12=6$

**[1]**

> *So each part is 6 cm. *
*Now multiply that by the ratio numbers to find the sizes of the three sides of the triangle.*

$3\times6=18\mathrm{cm}4\times6=24\mathrm{cm}5\times6=30\mathrm{cm}$

**[1]**

> *Now use the  *$\frac{1}{2}\times\mathrm{base}\times\mathrm{height}$*  formula for the area of a triangle. *
*In a right-angled triangle the two sides that are **not **the hypotenuse are the 'base' and 'height' for that formula. *
*And the longest side is the hypotenuse, so use 18 and 24 as the base and height.*

$\begin{aligned}Area & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 24 \\ & = & 216\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$216\mathrm{cm}^{2}$**  [1]**

Mary is going to cover the floor with tiles.

One pack of tiles will cover 2m<sup>2</sup>

Mary gets a discount of 25% off the cost of the tiles.

parts.solutionMd:
> *Split the shape of the floor into a rectangle and a trapezium.*

![4-5-29](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/area-and-perimeter/assets/067-4-5-29.png)

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 2 . 2 \times 3 \\ & = & 6 . 6 m^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the area of the trapezium, using the formula: *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the lengths of the parallel sides and *$h$*is the perpendicular height.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & \frac{1}{2} \left(3 + 1\right) \times 1 . 2 \\ & = & 2 . 4 m^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the total area of the floor by adding together the area of the rectangle and the trapezium.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 6 . 6 + 2 . 4 \\ & = & 9 m^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Calculate the number of packs of tiles that Mary will need by dividing the total floor area by the area covered by each pack of tiles.*

$\frac{9}{2}=4.5$* *
*Mary will need 5 packs of tiles*

$\begin{aligned}24 . 80 \times 0 . 75 & = & 18 . 60\end{aligned}$

> *Find the total cost of tiling the floor by multiplying the cost of the discounted packs of tiles by the number of packs required.*

$\begin{aligned}5 \times 18 . 60 & = & 93\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

**Yes, Mary has enough money to buy all the tiles she needs as she only needs £93 but has £100 available ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Here are two watch faces, **A** and **B**.

![q1-4-6-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/circles-arcs-and-sectors/assets/018-q1-4-6-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

Both watch faces are circular with radius 2cm.

The materials used to make both watch faces have the same thickness.

**A** is made entirely of plastic. 
**B** has a 20° sector of metal and a 340° sector of plastic.

The ratio of the cost per cm<sup>2</sup> of the metal to the cost per cm<sup>2</sup> of the plastic is 3 : 2

Work out the ratio of the cost of the materials for **A** to the cost of the materials for **B**. 
Give your answer in its simplest form. 
You must show all your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the area of face A, using the formula for the area of a circle: *$A=πr^{2}$*, where *$r$* is the radius of the circle.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & \pi \times 2^{2} \\ & = & 4 \pi cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Find the relative cost of the materials for face A by multiplying the area by 2.*

$\begin{aligned}C_{A} & = & 2 \times 2 \pi \\ & = & 8 \pi\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Calculate the area of the metal part of face B, using the formula for the area of a sector: *$A=\frac{θ^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}}\timesπr^{2}$*, where *$θ$* is the angle of the sector.*

$\begin{aligned}A_{m e t a l} & = & \frac{20}{360} \times \pi \times 2^{2} \\ & = & \frac{2}{9} \pi cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the area of the plastic part of face B by subtracting the area of the metal part from the area of the whole face.*

$\begin{aligned}A_{p l a s t i c} & = & 4 \pi - \frac{2}{9} \pi \\ & = & \frac{34}{9} \pi cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Find the relative cost of the materials for face B by multiplying the plastic area by 2 and the metal area by 3 and adding together.*

$\begin{aligned}C_{B} & = & 3 \times \frac{2}{9} \pi + 2 \times \frac{34}{9} \pi \\ & = & \frac{74}{9} \pi\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find a ratio for the cost of materials for face A to face B.*

$A:B\,8π:\frac{74}{9}π$

**[1]**

$8:\frac{74}{9}\,72:74$

$36:37$* ***[1]**

the perimeter of sector $OBC=2\times$the perimeter of triangle $OAD$

parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the perimeter of the triangle **OAD **by first using the cosine rule, *$a^{2} = b^{2} + c^{2} - 2 b c cos \left(A\right)$*.*

> *Substitute the values of the sides (both 6 cm) and angle (50°) into the cosine rule formula.*

$\begin{aligned}A D^{2} & = & 6^{2} + 6^{2} - \left(2 \times 6 \times 6 \times cos 50\right) \\ A D & = & \sqrt{ 6^{2} + 6^{2} - \left(2 \times 6 \times 6 \times cos 50\right)} \\ & = & 5 . 071419 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the perimeter of triangle **OAD.*

*Perimeter of ***OAD *** = 6 + 6 + 5.071419... = 17.071419... cm**<sup> </sup>*

**[1]**

> *Find the length of the arc **BC **using the formula for length of an arc *$=\frac{θ^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}}\times2πr$*. *
*Find an expression for the length of the arc in terms of *$x$*, **by substituting *$θ=50$* and *$r=(6+x)$*.*

$B C = \frac{50}{360} \times 2 \times \pi \times \left(x + 6\right)$

**[1]**

> *Find an expression for the perimeter of the sector **OBC** in terms of *$x$*, **by adding this to 2 × the radius.*

$\begin{aligned}O B C & = & \left( \frac{50}{360} \times 2 \times \pi \times \left(x + 6\right) \right) + 2 \left(x + 6\right) \\ & = & \frac{5}{18} \left(x + 6\right) \pi + 2 \left(x + 6\right) \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Form an equation by setting this equal to 2 times the perimeter of triangle **OAD**. *

$\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{18} \left(x + 6\right) \pi + 2 \left(x + 6\right) & = & 2 \left(17 . 071419 . . .\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify by expanding the brackets on both sides and collecting like terms.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{5 \pi}{18} x + \frac{5 \pi}{3} + 2 x + 12 & = & 34 . 14283 . . . \\ 2 . 872664 . . . x & = & 16 . 90684 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Solve the equation.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{16 . 90684 . . .}{2 . 872664 . . .} = 5 . 885422 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

$x=5.89$** cm**<sup>** **</sup>**(3 s.f.)**** [1] **
**Answers in the range 5.88 to 5.89 accepted.**

parts.solutionMd:
> *The area of the region **R **is the area of the larger segment from circle centre **O** added to the area of the smaller segment from circle centre **P**. *

$A r e a_{t r i a n g l e A O B} = \frac{1}{2} \times \left(5\right) \times \left(5\right) \times sin \left(50\right) = \frac{25}{2} sin 50$

> *It is best to leave working as exact values as you work through the problem, but if you choose to round make sure you use at least 4 significant figures throughout. *

> *Find the area of the sector **AOB **using the formula for area of a sector *$=\frac{θ}{360^{\circ}}\timesπr^{2}$*.*

> *Substitute the given values into the formula, letting *$θ=50$* and *$r=5$*.*

$\frac{50}{360}\timesπ\times5^{2}=\frac{125}{36}π$

**[1]**

> *Find the area of the segment by subtracting the area of triangle **AOB **from the area of sector **AOB.*

*Area segment (circle ***O***) =*$\frac{125}{36}π-\frac{25}{2}\mathrm{sin}50$

> *To find the area of the segment in circle centre **P, **we first need to find angle **APB.*

> *Triangles **AOB **and **APB **are both isosceles triangles so the line **OP **is a line of symmetry. The sine rule can be used with triangle **AOP **to find the value of angle **APO **which can then be doubled to find angle **APB.*

![ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q4-diagram-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/circles-arcs-and-sectors/assets/010-ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q4-diagram-2.png)

> *Use the sine rule with the angles on the numerators, *$\frac{\mathrm{sin}A}{a}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}B}{b}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}C}{c}$*.*

$\frac{sin \left(A P O\right)}{5} = \frac{sin \left(25\right)}{4}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 5 and use the inverse sin to find the angle **APO**.*

$\text{sin} A P O = 5 \times \frac{ \text{sin} 25}{4} = 0.528272...$
$\text{angle} A P O = \text{sin} ^{ - } 1 ( 0.528272... ) = 31.88883...$

**[1]**

> *Angle **APB **= 2 × angle **APO**.*

$A P B = 2 \left(31 . 88883 . . .\right) = 63 . 77766 . . .$

> *Find the area of triangle **APB** using the area of a triangle formula, *$A=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$*.*

$A r e a_{t r i a n g l e A P B} = \frac{1}{2} \times \left(4\right) \times \left(4\right) \times sin \left(63 . 77766 . . .\right) = 7 . 176689 . . .$

> *Find the area of the sector **APB **using the formula for area of a sector *$=\frac{θ}{360^{\circ}}\timesπr^{2}$*.*

$\frac{63.77766...}{360}\timesπ\times4^{2}=8.905041...$

**[1]**

> *Find the area of the segment by subtracting the area of triangle **APB **from the area of sector **APB.*

*Area segment (circle ***P***) = *$8.905041...-7.176689...=1.728352...$

> *Find the area of the shaded section by adding the area of the two segments together.*

*Area shaded = *$\left(\frac{125}{36} \pi - \frac{25}{2} sin 50\right) + 1 . 728352 . . . = 3 . 061104 . . .$

**[1]**

> *Round the final answer to 3 significant figures. *

**Area = 3.06 cm**<sup>**2**</sup>** ****[1] **
**Answers in the range 3 to 3.1 accepted**

Give your answer in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First convert the ratios for each radius into fractions of the length of **OP** and **OQ.*

**OA ***= *$\frac{3}{3+2}=\frac{3}{5}$* of ***OP***.*

**OB ***= *$\frac{3}{3+2}=\frac{3}{5}$* of ***OQ***.*

> *Write **OA,** **OB**, **OP** and **OQ** in terms of **r.** *

$\mathrm{Let}OP=OQ=r\,\mathrm{Then}OA=OB=\frac{3}{5}r$

> *Find an expression in terms of **r **for the area of the sector **OPQ **using the formula for the area of a sector *$=\frac{θ}{360^{\circ}}\timesπr^{2}$*.*

$\mathrm{Area}OPQ=\frac{45}{360}\timesπ\timesr^{2}$

> *Find an expression in terms of **r **for the area of the sector **OAB **using the formula for the area of a sector *$=\frac{θ}{360^{\circ}}\timesπr^{2}$*.*

$Area O A B = \frac{45}{360} \times \pi \times \left(\frac{3}{5} r\right)^{2}$

** ****Either expression correct ****[1]**

> *Find an expression in terms of **r **for the area of the shaded region by subtracting the area of sector **OAB **from the area of sector **OPQ.*

$Area shaded = \frac{45}{360} \pi \times r^{2} - \frac{45}{360} \pi \times \left(\frac{3}{5} r\right)^{2} = \frac{45}{360} \pi \left(r^{2} - \left(\frac{3}{5} r\right)^{2}\right)$

> *Form an equation in terms of **r **for the area of the shaded region by setting it equal to *$\frac{81}{2}π$*.*

$\frac{45}{360} \pi \left(\frac{16}{25} r^{2}\right) = \frac{81}{2} \pi$

**[1]**

> *Simplify and divide both sides by*$π$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{25} \cancel{\pi} r^{2} & = & \frac{81}{2} \cancel{\pi} \\ r^{2} & = & \frac{81}{2} \div \frac{2}{25}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Use your calculator to find the value of **r**. *

$\begin{aligned}r & = & \sqrt{\frac{81}{2} \div \frac{2}{25}} = 22 . 5\end{aligned}$

> *Find the perimeter of the shaded section by calculating the arc length of the larger arc (**PQ**) and the smaller arc (**AB**) using the formula for the arc length of a sector: *$\mathrm{Arc} \mathrm{length}=\frac{θ^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}}\times2πr$*, where *$r$* radius of the circle and *$θ$* is the angle of the sector.*

$\begin{aligned}Arc length_{P Q} & = & \frac{45}{360} \times 2 \times \pi \times 22 . 5\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}Arc length_{A B} & = & \frac{45}{360} \times 2 \times \pi \times \left(\frac{3}{5} \times 22 . 5\right)\end{aligned}$

** ****Either correct ****[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}Arc length_{P Q} & = & \frac{45}{8} \pi\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}Arc length_{A B} & = & \frac{27}{8} \pi\end{aligned}$

> *Find **AP **and **BQ **using the differences in the radius for **OA **and **OB.*

> * *$\begin{aligned}A P & = & B Q = 22 . 5 - \frac{3}{5} \left(22 . 5\right) = 9 cm\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the perimeter of the shaded segment by adding the arc lengths together along with the lengths of the straight edges joining them. *

$\begin{aligned}P & = & \frac{45}{8} \pi + \frac{27}{8} \pi + 9 + 9\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The answer should be left in terms of **π**, so simplify both parts separately.*

$\begin{aligned}P & = & \left(\frac{45}{8} + \frac{27}{8}\right) \pi + \left(9 + 9\right)\end{aligned}$

$P=9π+18\mathrm{cm}$* ***[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *The area of the shaded region is the area of the triangle subtracted from the area of the sector.*

> *Find the area of the triangle using the area of a triangle formula, *$A=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the two known sides and *$C$* is the included angle. The two sides** **are both radii so are both equal to 5 cm and the angle is equal to 60°.*

$Area_{triangle} = \frac{1}{2} \times \left(5\right) \times \left(5\right) \times sin \left(60\right) = \frac{25}{2} sin 60$

**[1]**

> *This is a non-calculator paper so leave working as exact values as you work through the problem. The exact value of sin 60° is *$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$*. Use this to simplify the expression for the area of the triangle, leaving it in terms of **π.*

$Area_{triangle} = \frac{25}{2} \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \frac{25 \sqrt{3}}{4}$

*Area segment  = *$\frac{25}{6}π-\frac{25\sqrt{3}}{4}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract the fractions by first finding the lowest common denominator, and adjusting the numerators accordingly.*

> *The lowest common denominator is 12. (LCM of 6 and 4 = 12). Set both fractions over 12, multiplying the numerator of the first by 2 and the second by 3.*

$\frac{2 \left(25\right)}{12} \pi - \frac{3 \left(25 \sqrt{3}\right)}{12}$

> *Simplify by subtracting the numerators.*

$\frac{50π}{12}-\frac{75\sqrt{3}}{12}$

**Final answer:** $\frac{50π-75\sqrt{3}}{12}$** ****[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for the circumference of a circle is *$2πr=\mathrm{πd}$*. *
*Find an expression for the circumference of the circle in terms of *$r.$

$C=2πr$* *

> *The perimeter of the sector is equal to the arc length of the sector plus the two straight edges (both radii).*

*The arc length of a sector (the length of the curved side) with radius *$r$* and angle *$θ$*° is *$\frac{θ}{360}\times2πr$*.* 
*Find an expression for the arc length of the sector by substituting *$θ=x$* and *$r=r$* into the formula.*

$\mathrm{Arc} \mathrm{length}=\frac{x}{360}\times2π\timesr=\frac{2πrx}{360}$

> *Find an expression for the perimeter of the sector by adding *$2r$* for the two straight edges.*

$\mathrm{Perimeter}=\frac{2πrx}{360}+2r$

> *Form an equation by setting the expressions for the circumference of the circle equal to the perimeter of the sector.*

$2πr=\frac{2πrx}{360}+2r$

**[1]**

> *Begin to simplify by dividing both sides by 2**r.*

$\begin{aligned}\cancel{2} \pi \cancel{r} & = & \frac{\cancel{2} \pi \cancel{r} x}{360} + \cancel{2 r} \\ \pi & = & \frac{\pi x}{360} + 1\end{aligned}$

> *Rearrange to make **x **the subject. *

$\begin{aligned}\pi - 1 & = & \frac{\pi x}{360} \\ 360 \left(\pi - 1\right) & = & \pi x \end{aligned}$

$x=\frac{360(π-1)}{π}$** ****[1] **

You know the length of the hypotenuse (**H**) and you want the length of the side that is opposite (**O**) the angle. Therefore you can use the sine ratio: *$\mathrm{sin}θ=\frac{O}{H}$*.*

parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the arc length of the smaller (inner) semi-circle by using the formula for the perimeter of a semi-circle: *$P = \frac{1}{2} \left(2 \pi r\right)$*where *$r$* is the radius of the circle.*

$\begin{aligned}L e ngth_{s m a l l a r c} & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times \pi \times 7\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}Length_{s m a l l a r c} & = & 7 \pi cm\end{aligned}$

> *The radius of the larger semi-circle is 2 cm more than the radius of the smaller semi-circle.*

> *Calculate the radius of the larger semi-circle.*

$7+2=9\mathrm{cm}$

> *Calculate the arc length of the larger (outer) semi-circle by using the formula for the perimeter of a semi-circle: *$P = \frac{1}{2} \left(2 \pi r\right)$*where *$r$* is the radius of the circle.*

$\begin{aligned}L e ngth_{l a r g e a r c} & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times \pi \times 9\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}Length_{l a r g e a r c} & = & 9 \pi cm\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the perimeter of the shaded segment by adding the arc lengths together along with the lengths of the straight edges joining them (2 cm each). *

$\begin{aligned}P & = & 7 \pi + 9 \pi + 2 + 2\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}P & = & 54 . 26548 . . . cm\end{aligned}$

> *Round to one decimal place.*

> *The first digit after the decimal point is 2 and the digit following it is 6, which is 5 or more you will need to round the 2 up. *

$54. \dot{2}\dot{6} 548... = 54.3 ( 1 \text{ d.p.} )$

**54.3 cm ****[1] **

parts.solutionMd:
> *The unshaded area can be found by subtracting the area of the semi-circle from the area of the circle.*

> *Find the area of the circle, the formula for the area of a circle is *$πr^{2}$*.*

> *It's best to keep your working in terms of *$π$* to preserve the accuracy of your final answer.*

$A r e a_{\left(c i r c l e\right)} = \pi \times 10^{2} = 100 \pi$* *

**[1]**

> *Find the area of the shaded region (semicircle) using the formula *$\frac{1}{2}πr^{2}$*. The radius of the semicircle is half of the diameter of the semicircle.*

$A r e a_{\left(s e m i c i r c l e\right)} = \frac{1}{2} \pi \left(\frac{8}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \pi \left(4\right)^{2} = \frac{16}{2} \pi = 8 \pi$

**[1]**

> *The area of the unshaded region = Area (circle) - Area (semicircle).*

$A r e a_{\left(c i r c l e\right)} - A r e a_{\left(s e m i c i r c l e\right)} = 100 \pi - 8 \pi = 92 \pi$

**[1]**

> *So the shaded area is 8**π **and the unshaded area is 92**π.  **Find how many times 92**π **is bigger than 8**π **by dividing 92 by 8.*

$\frac{92π}{8π}=\frac{92}{8}=11.5$

**The unshaded area is 11.5 times bigger than the shaded area ****[1]**

....................................... newtons
parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:

 The average speed of the plane was $650$ kilometres per hour.

**[1]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd:
![q3-medium-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/standard-and-compound-units/assets/002-q3-medium-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edexce.png)

$A,B$ and $C$ are 3 service stations on a motorway.

$AB$ = 25 miles 
$BC$ = 25 miles

Aysha drives along the motorway from $A$ to $C$

Aysha drives at an average speed of 50 mph from $A$ to $B$. 
She drives at an average speed of 60 mph from $B$ to $C$.

Work out the difference in the time Aysha takes to drive from $A$ to $B$ and the time Aysha takes to drive from$B$ to $C$. 
Give your answer in minutes.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use  Time = Distance ÷ Speed  to find Aysha's times from **A** to **B **and from **B** to **C**. *
*It's easiest to convert to minutes at this point.  (Remember there are 60 minutes in an hour!)*

$\begin{aligned}A to B : \frac{25}{50} & = & \frac{1}{2} hour = 30 minutes \\ & & \\ B to C : \frac{25}{60} & = & \frac{5}{12} hours \\ \frac{5}{12} hours & = & \frac{5}{12} \times 60 = 25 minutes\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now subtract to find the difference in times.*

$30-25=5$

**[1]**

**5 minutes****  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
Sue is driving home from her friend's house.

Sue drives

10 miles from her friend's house to the motorway       
      240 miles on the motorway       
      5 miles from the motorway to her home

Sue

takes 20 minutes to drive from her friend's house to the motorway       
       drives at an average speed of 60 mph on the motorway       
        takes 25 minutes to drive from the motorway to her home

Sue stops for a 30 minute rest on her drive home.

Sue leaves her friend's house at 9.00 am.

What time does Sue get home? You must show all your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use  Time = Distance ÷ Speed  to find how long Sue was driving on the motorway.*

$\begin{aligned}240 \div 60 & = & 4 hours\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now add the times together to find her total travel time. Remember that there are 60 minutes in an hour.*

$20+25+30=75\mathrm{minutes}=1h15m\,\,1h15m+4h=5h15m$

**[1]**

> *Finally add that time onto 9.00 am to find out when she arrived home. 3 hours takes the time up to 12.00 noon, and the remaining 2 h 15 m takes it to 2.15 pm.*

**2.15 pm****  [1]**

**1415 (the 24 hour clock version) will also get the mark here**

parts.problemMd:
A gold bar has a mass of 12.5 kg. 
The density of gold is 19.3 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.

Work out the volume of the gold bar. 
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:

*(Remember there are 1000 g in a kg.)*

$\begin{aligned}12 . 5 \times 1000 & = & 12500 g \\ & & \\ 12500 \div 19 . 3 & = & 647 . 668393 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[2] **
**1 mark for using Volume = Mass ÷ Density.  1 mark for converting kg to g.**

> *Round to 3 s.f. (and remember your units!).*

**648 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>**  [1]**
** ****Answers in range 647 to 648 will get the mark here.**

parts.problemMd:
$\mathrm{Pressure}=\frac{\mathrm{force}}{\mathrm{area}}$

Find the pressure extered by a force of 900 newtons on an area of 60cm<sup>2</sup>. 
Give your answer in newtons/m<sup>2</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First convert the area to m*<sup>*2*</sup>*, to match the units asked for in the answer. *
*Remember that 1 m*<sup>*2*</sup>* = (100 cm) × (100 cm) = (100 × 100) cm*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$\frac{60}{100\times100}=\frac{60}{10000}=0.006m^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Now put the force and the converted area into the formula given.*

**150000 newtons/m**<sup>**2**</sup>**  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
Tame Valley is a company that makes yoghurt.

A machine fills trays of 20 pots with yoghurt. In one hour, the machine fills a total of 15 000 pots.

Work out how many seconds the machine takes to fill each tray of 20 pots.
parts.solutionMd:
> *We want the answer to be in seconds per tray. Start by converting 1 hour into seconds. Remember that there are 60 minutes in an hour, and 60 seconds in a minute.*

$1\mathrm{hour}=60\mathrm{minutes}=60\times60=3600\mathrm{seconds}$

**[1]**

> *Now divide 15000 by 20 to find how many trays are filled in an hour.*

$15000\div20=750\mathrm{trays} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{hour}$

**[1]**

> *Finally divide 3600 by 750 to find the number of seconds per tray.*

$3600\div750=4.8$

**[1]**

**4.8 seconds****  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
There are 18500 gallons of fuel in a fuel tank.

The fuel is pumped from the fuel tank into a plane at a rate of 1700 litres per minute.

1 gallon = 4.5 litres.

How many minutes will it take to empty the fuel tank completely? Give your answer to the nearest minute.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The fuel pumping rate is given in litres per minute. Start by converting 18500 gallons into litres. Each gallon has 4.5 litres, so **multiply** 18500 by 4.5.*

$18500\times4.5=83250\mathrm{litres}$

**[1]**

> *And each minute, 1700 litres of fuel are pumped. So **divide** 83250 by 1700 to find the number of minutes.*

$83250\div1700=48.970588...\mathrm{minutes}$

**[1]**

> *Finally round to the nearest minute as asked for in the question.*

**49 minutes****  [1]**

**Answers in the range 48.9 - 49.1 will get the mark here.**

parts.problemMd:
Axel and Lethna are driving along a motorway.

They see a road sign. The road sign shows the distance to Junction 8 It also shows the average time drivers take to get to Junction 8

| To Junction 8 30 miles 26 minutes |
|---|

The speed limit on the motorway is 70 mph.

Lethna says      
 "We will have to drive faster than the speed limit to drive 30 miles in 26 minutes."

Is Lethna right? 
You must show how you get your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by converting '30 miles in 26 minutes' into miles per minute.*

$30\div26=\frac{15}{13}\mathrm{miles} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{minute}$

**[1]**

> *So they would need to travel 15/13 miles every minute. And there are 60 minutes in an hour. So **multiply** that speed by 60 to convert to miles per hour.*

$\frac{15}{13} \times 60 = 69 . 230769 . . . = 69 . 2 mph \left(3 s . f .\right)$

**[1]**

> *Express your results in the context of the question.*

**30 miles in 26 minutes corresponds to an average speed of 69.2 mph.  So Lethna is not correct.****  [1]**

**You can also earn full marks by showing that going 70 mph for 26 minutes means you will go 30.333... miles. Or by showing that at 70 mph, it will only take 25.714... minutes to travel 30 miles.**

parts.problemMd:
Change a speed of 50 metres per second to a speed in kilometres per hour.

.......................... kilometres per hour
parts.solutionMd:
*Convert each unit separately.* 
*There are 60 seconds in a minute. Multiply by 60 to find how many metres are travelled in a minute.*

$\begin{aligned}50 metres per second & = & 50 \times 60 metres per minute \\ & = & 3000 metres per minute\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *There are 60 minutes in an hour. Multiply by 60 to find how many metres are travelled in an hour.*

$\begin{aligned}3000 metres per minute & = & 3000 \times 60 metres per hour \\ & = & 180000 metres per hour\end{aligned}$

> *There are 1000 metres in a kilometre. Divide by 1000 to find how many kilometres are travelled in an hour.*

$\begin{aligned}18000 metres per hour & = & \frac{180000}{1000} kilometres per hour\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$180\mathrm{kilometres} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{hour}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A block of wood has a mass of $3.5\mathrm{kg}$. 
The wood has density $0.65\mathrm{kg}/m^{3}$

Work out the volume of the block of wood. 
Give your answer correct to $3$ significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
$\mathrm{Density}=\frac{\mathrm{Mass}}{\mathrm{Volume}}.$* If you forget this formula then you can derive it using the units for density, kg/m*<sup>*3*</sup>*. Kilograms measure a mass and cubic metres measure a volume.* 
*Substitute 0.65 for the density and 3.5 for the mass.*

$0.65=\frac{3.5}{\mathrm{Volume}}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by the volume and divide both sides by 0.65.*

$\begin{aligned}Volume & = & \frac{3 . 5}{0 . 65} \\ & = & \frac{70}{13} \\ & = & 5 . 384615 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures. Your answer will be in cubic metres.*

**Volume is 5.38 m**<sup>**3**</sup>** (3sf)** **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Change a speed of $630$ kilometres per hour to a speed in metres per second.
parts.solutionMd:
*Convert each unit separately.* 
*There are 60 seconds in a minute. Divide by 60 to find how many kilometres are travelled in a minute.*

$\begin{aligned}630 kilometres per hour & = & \frac{ 630 }{60} kilometres per minute \\ & = & 10 . 5 kilometres per minute\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *There are 60 minutes in an hour. Divide by 60 to find how many kilometres are travelled in a second.*

$\begin{aligned}10 . 5 kilometres per minute & = & \frac{ 10 . 5 }{60} kilometres per second \\ & = & 0 . 175 kilometres per second\end{aligned}$

> *There are 1000 metres in a kilometre. Multiply by 1000 to find how many metres are travelled in a second.*

$\begin{aligned}0 . 175 kilometres per second & = & 1000 \times 0 . 175 metres per second\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$175\mathrm{metres} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{second}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$\mathrm{Density}=\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{volume}}$

The mass is divided by 2 and the volume is multiplied by 4 What happens to the density? Circle your answer.

| $\times2$ | $\div2$ | $\times8$ | $\div8$ |
|---|---|---|---|
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

*If the top of a fraction gets smaller then the overall value of the fraction also gets smaller. Therefore dividing the mass by 2 causes the density to be divided by 2.* 
*If the bottom of a fraction gets bigger then the overall value of the fraction gets smaller. Therefore multiplying the volume by 4 causes the density to be divided by 4.* 
*Combine both effects, dividing by 2 then dividing by 4 is equivalent to dividing by 8.*

**÷ 8** **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Use actual numbers. Say the mass is 100 and the volume is 1.*

$\mathrm{Density}=\frac{100}{1}=100$

> *Divide the mass by 2 and multiply the volume by 4 and calculate the new density.*

$\mathrm{Density}=\frac{100\div2}{1\times4}=\frac{50}{4}=12.5$

> *Choose the option takes you from 100 to 12.5.*

**÷ 8** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Which **one** of these is a unit of density? Circle your answer.

| $\mathrm{kg}/m^{2}$ | $m^{2}/\mathrm{kg}$ | $\mathrm{kg}/m^{3}$ | $m^{3}/\mathrm{kg}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
parts.solutionMd:
> *Density measures how heavy something is per a unit of volume. The formula is *$\mathrm{Desnity}=\frac{\mathrm{Mass}}{\mathrm{Volume}}.$* Kilograms (kg) is a measure of mass and cubic metres (m*<sup>*3*</sup>*) is a measure of volume, therefore kg/m*<sup>*3*</sup>* is a measure of density.*

**kg/m**<sup>**3**</sup>** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
Arron ran a distance of 5 km at an average speed of 2.2 m/s.

How long did Arron run for? 
                   Give your answer in minutes and seconds, to the nearest second.

.............. minutes ................ seconds
parts.solutionMd:
> *The measurements need to use consistent units. 1 km = 1000 m so convert 5 km to m.*

$5\mathrm{km}=5000m$

* ***[1]**

> $\mathrm{Average} \mathrm{Speed}=\frac{\mathrm{Distance}}{\mathrm{Time}}.$* Substitute 5000 for the distance and 2.2 for the speed.*

$2.2=\frac{5000}{\mathrm{Time}}$

> *Rearrange by multiplying both sides by the time and dividing both sides by 2.2. The units for the time will be seconds.*

$\begin{aligned}Time & = & \frac{5000}{2 . 2} \\ & = & 2272 . 727 . . . s\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Round to the nearest second.*

$2273s$

$\frac{2273}{60}=37.83333...$

* ***[1]**

> *This 37 minutes. Convert the decimal part to seconds by subtracting the integer part and multiplying by 60.*

$0.83333...\times60=53$

**37 minutes 53 seconds**** (nearest second)** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Henry is thinking of having a water meter. These are the two ways he can pay for the water he uses. | **Water Meter** A charge of £28.20 per year

**plus** 91.22p for every cubic metre of water used

1 cubic metre = 1000 litres | |---| | **No Water Meter** A charge of £107 per year | |---| Henry uses an average of 180 litres of water each day. Use this information to determine whether or not Henry should have a water meter.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First divide 180 by 1000 to find out how many cubic metres Henry uses each day.*

$180\div1000=0.18\mathrm{cubic} \mathrm{metres}$

**[1]**

> *Now multiply by 91.22p to find the cost per day with the water meter.*

$0 . 18 \times 91 . 22 = 16 . 4196 p = \pounds 0 . 164196$

**[1]**

> *Then multiply by 365 (the number of days in a normal year) to find the price for water used per year. (You don't need to worry about leap years here!)*

$0 . 164196 \times 365 = \pounds 59 . 93154$

**[1]**

> *Add £28.20 to find the total cost with a water meter per year.*

$59 . 93154 + 28 . 20 = 88 . 13154 = \pounds 88 . 13 \left(nearest penny\right)$

**[1]**

> *And finally interpret your results in the context of the question.*

**It will cost Henry £88.13 per year with the water meter, which is cheaper than the £107 without the meter.  Therefore he should have a water meter.****  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
The distance from Fulbeck to Ganby is 10 miles. The distance from Ganby to Horton is 18 miles.

![q3-hard-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/shape-space-and-measure/standard-and-compound-units/assets/001-q3-hard-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edexcel-.png)

Raksha is going to drive from Fulbeck to Ganby. 
Then she will drive from Ganby to Horton.

Raksha leaves Fulbeck at 10 00 
She drives from Fulbeck to Ganby at an average speed of 40 mph.

Raksha wants to get to Horton at 10 35 
Work out the average speed Raksha must drive at from Ganby to Horton.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First find out how long it takes her to go from Fulbeck to Ganby. Use the formula  Time = Distance ÷ Speed. *
*It's easiest to convert to minutes at this point.  (Remember there are 60 minutes in an hour!)*

$\frac{10}{40}=\frac{1}{4}\mathrm{hour}=15\mathrm{minutes}$

**[1]**

> *10.00 to 10.35 is 35 minutes, so subtract 15 from 35 to find how many minutes she has to get from Ganby to Horton. *
*Then divide 18 by that to see how many miles per minute she needs to go. *
*And multiply that by 60 to convert miles per minute to miles per hour.*

$35-15=20\mathrm{minutes}\,\,\frac{18}{20}=0.9\mathrm{miles} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{minute}\,\,0.9\times60=54$

**[1]**

**54 mph****  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
Liquid A has a density of 0.7 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.

140 g of liquid A and 128 g of liquid B are mixed to make liquid C.

Work out the density of liquid C.

$140+128=268g$

**[1]**

*Then add those together to find the volume of Liquid C.*

$\mathrm{Liquid}A:\frac{140}{0.7}=200\mathrm{cm}^{3}\,\,\mathrm{Liquid}B:\frac{128}{1.6}=80\mathrm{cm}^{3}\,\,200+80=280\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Use  Density = Mass ÷ Volume  to find the density of Liquid C.*

$\frac{268}{280}=0.957142...$

**[1]**

** **

**0.957 g/cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** (3 s.f.)****  [1]**

**Answers between 0.957 and 0.96 will get the mark here**

parts.problemMd:

 Tin has a density of 7.31 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.

Work out the density of the alloy. 
Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use  Volume = Mass ÷ Density  to find the volumes of lead and tin.*

$\mathrm{lead}:\frac{74}{11.34}=6.5255...\mathrm{cm}^{3}\,\,\mathrm{tin}:\frac{126}{7.31}=17.2366...\mathrm{cm}$

**[1] **
**Mark is for using Volume = Mass ÷ Density to try to find either volume**

> *Now add the volumes together to find the total volume of the alloy. *
*Then use  Density = Mass ÷ Volume  to find the density of the alloy.*

$6.5255...+17.2366...=23.7622...\mathrm{cm}^{3}\,\,\frac{200}{23.7622...}=8.4167...$

**[1]**

parts.problemMd:
David has designed a game. 
He uses a fair 6-sided dice and a fair 5-sided spinner. 
The dice is numbered 1 to 6 
The spinner is numbered 1 to 5

Each player rolls the dice once and spins the spinner once. 
A player can win £5 or win £2

![q1-5-4-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/statistics-and-probability/combined-and-conditional-probability/assets/001-q1-5-4-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

David expects 30 people will play his game. 
Each person will pay David £1 to play the game.

Work out how much profit David can expect to make.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First find the probabilities for winning each of the prizes. In combined probabilities, 'and' usually means 'multiply' and 'or' usually means 'add'. *
*'Roll a 5 AND spin a 5' is P(roll 5)*$\times$*P(spin 5). *
*'Roll a 1 OR spin a 1 OR both' is the same as 'roll a 1 AND spin a 1' OR 'roll a 1 AND don't spin a 1' OR 'don't roll a 1 AND spin a 1'.  *
*So the probability is (P(roll 1)*$\times$*P(spin 1)) + (P(roll 1)*$\times$*P(don't spin 1)) + (P(don't roll 1)*$\times$*P(spin 1)).*

$\mathrm{P} ( \text{win} £ 5 ) = \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{5} = \frac{1}{30}$

$\mathrm{P} ( \text{win} £ 2 ) = ( \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{5} ) + ( \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{4}{5} ) + ( \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{1}{5} ) = \frac{1}{3}$


**[1]**

> *Now find the total prize money David is likely to have to pay out. 30*$\times$*P(win £5) people are expected to win £5. *
*30*$\times$*P(win £2) people are expected to win £2.*

$\begin{aligned}expected payout & = & \left(\left(30 \times \frac{1}{30}\right) \times \pounds 5\right) + \left(\left(30 \times \frac{1}{3}\right) \times \pounds 2\right) \\ & = & \pounds 5 + \pounds 20 \\ & = & \pounds 25 \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *He expects to receive £30, from 30 people each paying £1 to play. *
*Subtract £25 from that to find his expected profit.*

$30-25=5$

**[1]**

**£5 *** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Give a reason why David's actual profit may be different to the profit he expects to make.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remember that probabilities are only likelihoods.  They can't say what **definitely** will happen.*

**The probabilities only say what is likely to happen.  What actually happens may be different. *** ***[1]**

**Other sensible answers can also get the mark here.  For example, saying that David expects 30 people to play, but that a different number may actually play.**

parts.problemMd:
Four friends each throw a biased coin a number of times. The table shows the number of heads and the number of tails each friend got.

|   | **Ben** | **Helen** | **Paul** | **Sharif** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| heads | 34 | 66 | 80 | 120 |
| tails | 8 | 12 | 40 | 40 |

The coin is to be thrown one more time.

Which of the four friends' results will give the best estimate for the probability that the coin will land heads?
Justify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *To determine experimental probabilities, an experiment should be repeated as many times as possible.  The more repetitions, the more reliable the results.*

**Sharif's results will give the best estimate, because he threw the coin the greatest number of times****  ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Paul says,

"With this coin you are twice as likely to get heads as to get tails."

Is Paul correct? 
Justify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Look at the results of heads versus tails for each of the friends, then use that to reach your conclusion.*

$\mathrm{Paul} \mathrm{heads}:\mathrm{tails}=80:40=2:1=\mathrm{twice} \mathrm{as} \mathrm{likely}\,\,\mathrm{Ben} \mathrm{heads}:\mathrm{tails}=34:8=17:4=\mathrm{more} \mathrm{than}4\mathrm{times} \mathrm{as} \mathrm{likely}\,\,\mathrm{Helen} \mathrm{heads}:\mathrm{tails}=66:12=33:6=\mathrm{more} \mathrm{than}5\mathrm{times} \mathrm{as} \mathrm{likely}\,\,\mathrm{Sharif} \mathrm{heads}:\mathrm{tails}=120:40=3:1=3\mathrm{times} \mathrm{as} \mathrm{likely}\,$*                          *

**[1]**

**Paul's statement is true for his own results, but it is not true for the other friends' results.  Therefore Paul is not correct.****  ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The coin is to be thrown twice.

Use all the results in the table to work out an estimate for the probability that the coin will land heads both times.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First find the relative frequency (i.e., experimental probability) for 'heads', by dividing the total number of times the coin landed on heads by the total number of times it was thrown. Then multiply that relative frequency by itself to determine an estimate for the probability the coin will land on heads the first time and then on heads again the second time.*

$\mathrm{P} ( \text{heads} ) = \frac{34 + 66 + 80 + 120}{34 + 66 + 80 + 120 + 8 + 12 + 40 + 40} = \frac{300}{400} = \frac{3}{4}$

$\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{9}{16}$*                          *

**[1]**

$\frac{9}{16}$**  ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:

Whose results will give the best estimate for the probability that the drawing pin will land point up? 
Give a reason for your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
